meta.blurb: Before every concert, Iris's heart races and her breath turns quick and high. Her friend Dev, a lung physiotherapist, explains the nose, the lungs and the diaphragm, and is honest about which breathing claims are stronger than the evidence.
meta.bible: Iris: a choir singer in her thirties whose breathing goes fast and high when she is nervous. Dev: her friend, a respiratory physiotherapist, warm, practical and honest about what is not proven. They talk in the rehearsal hall, a Park, and Dev's clinic over Six weeks before a big concert called the Winter Concert. Key terms: Diaphragm, Alveoli, Bronchi, Oxygen, Carbon dioxide, Haemoglobin, Nasal cycle, Nitric oxide, Cilia, Mucus, Hyperventilation, Asthma, Inhaler, Apnoea, Altitude, Vagus, Humming. Real science only, hedged where research is modest or uncertain: no invented numbers or studies, and the book says plainly that many claims online are stronger than the evidence. Voice: calm, kind, plain, a little humorous. Nobody gets personal medical advice; the book gives general information and tells readers to see a doctor about their own health. Added in the full-length book: Mara, the choir director, brisk and kind, who conducts the Winter Concert; Sam, a tenor in the choir who has Asthma and uses his Inhaler as his doctor taught him; Edith, eighty-one, the oldest alto in the choir, who sings with a long steady breath; Tom, Iris's uncle, who stopped Smoking at sixty. The last song of the concert is called Snow Light and has one very long phrase. The Winter Concert is in a town hall; Dev's Clinic has a small Gym room and a plant by the window. Iris works at a desk in a small office, where she types for hours. The six weeks run from the first rehearsal to the concert night, and Dev meets Iris twice a week. More terms: Windpipe, Epiglottis, Trachea, Larynx, Vocal folds, Brainstem, Intercostal muscles, Capillaries, Pleura, Wheeze, Cough, Snoring, Yawn, Posture, Pollution, Particles, Ventilation, Acclimatisation, Cyclic sighing, Box breathing, Lip trill, Rebreathing, Nostril, Sinus, Sinuses, Larynx, Cartilage, Reflex, Hiccup, Hiccups, Sigh, Vaping, Spirometry, Pulse, Heartbeat, Adrenaline, Cortisol. Beats are told in the order of the six weeks. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: Iris stands in a concert hall wing with a hand on her fast-moving chest
beats.summary: Before a rehearsal, Iris feels her heart race and her breath turn quick and high.

beats.scene: Mara the director stands before the choir with a score and a raised baton
beats.summary: Mara, the choir director, announces the Winter Concert in six weeks and its hardest song, Snow Light.

beats.scene: Singers in rows hold open scores while one woman gasps for air mid-note
beats.summary: In the first run through Snow Light, Iris runs out of breath in the middle of the long phrase.

beats.scene: Dev in a cardigan hands Iris a cup of water in the empty hall
beats.summary: Her friend Dev, a lung physiotherapist, notices and says breathing is a skill that can be learned.

beats.scene: Dev and Iris sit with a notebook on two chairs in a half-lit hall
beats.summary: Dev offers to meet her often until the concert and promises to be honest about what science does not know.

beats.scene: A tally of twenty thousand tiny dots rises above a sleeping figure
beats.summary: Dev starts with a surprising number: about twenty thousand breaths in a single day.

beats.scene: Iris sits with a watch on her wrist and counts breaths on her fingers
beats.summary: Dev asks Iris to count her breaths for one minute and she is surprised by the result.

beats.scene: Cells like tiny furnaces glow as small blue dots flow in to feed them
beats.summary: We breathe because the body's cells burn fuel to make energy, and they need oxygen to do it.

beats.scene: Tiny arrows carry oxygen into a body and carbon dioxide out of it
beats.summary: The burning leaves a waste gas, carbon dioxide, and breathing delivers one gas and removes the other.

beats.scene: Iris walks home under streetlights, a hand on her stomach
beats.summary: Dev's first task: simply notice the breath three times a day, without trying to change it.

beats.scene: A plastic model of lungs and a windpipe sits on a clinic desk
beats.summary: In Dev's clinic, a plastic model of the lungs starts the tour of a breath.

beats.scene: Air enters a nose and mouth and slides down a throat
beats.summary: Air enters through the nose or the mouth and passes down the throat.

beats.scene: A small flap closes over a tube like a lid as food slides past
beats.summary: A small flap, the epiglottis, covers the windpipe when we swallow so that food goes to the stomach.

beats.scene: Iris touches the front of her neck while Dev points at the windpipe
beats.summary: The windpipe, or trachea, is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage that Iris can feel on her own neck.

beats.scene: The windpipe divides into two tubes, a larger one going to the right lung
beats.summary: The windpipe divides into two tubes called bronchi, one for each lung.

beats.scene: A branching tree shape grows upside down inside a chest
beats.summary: The airways branch again and again like an upside-down tree, into smaller and smaller tubes.

beats.scene: Tiny bubbles like grapes cluster at the end of a thin tube
beats.summary: At the end of the smallest tubes are hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

beats.scene: A red blood vessel wraps a thin-walled air sac while small dots pass through
beats.summary: Oxygen passes through the very thin walls of the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out.

beats.scene: A red blood cell carries small blue dots and glows with an iron-coloured core
beats.summary: Red blood cells carry oxygen with a substance called haemoglobin, which also gives blood its colour.

beats.scene: A heart pumps red blood along arrows toward a leg muscle and back
beats.summary: The heart pumps the oxygen-rich blood around the body, and a full circuit takes roughly a minute.

beats.scene: Dev holds a soft sponge beside the lung model and squeezes it
beats.summary: Dev asks what pulls air into the lungs, and explains that the lungs have no muscles of their own.

beats.scene: A dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs flattens as a belly softens outward
beats.summary: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, and when it contracts it flattens and pulls air in.

beats.scene: A chest drawn as a box whose floor drops while arrows rush in
beats.summary: When the chest space grows, the pressure inside drops and air flows in from outside.

beats.scene: A bottle model with a balloon inside and a rubber sheet pulled down
beats.summary: Dev builds a bottle model with a balloon and a rubber sheet that shows how a bigger space draws air in.

beats.scene: A relaxed dome rises as a gentle arrow of air leaves the nose
beats.summary: At rest, breathing out is mostly passive: the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic lungs spring back.

beats.scene: Iris lies on a mat with a small book rising on her belly
beats.summary: Dev asks Iris to lie down with a book on her belly and she sees it rise as the diaphragm moves down.

beats.scene: Ribs spread like a basket as small muscles between them lift the chest
beats.summary: The ribs also move: small muscles between them lift the ribs like bucket handles as we breathe in.

beats.scene: Iris breathes high with raised shoulders while Dev points at her neck muscles
beats.summary: When we breathe hard or anxiously, muscles in the neck and shoulders join in, and Iris notices hers lift.

beats.scene: A figure hiccups while a dome jumps like a trampoline
beats.summary: A hiccup is a sudden jerk of the diaphragm followed by the voice box snapping shut, and it usually passes alone.

beats.scene: Dev draws the full path from nose to diaphragm on a whiteboard
beats.summary: Dev draws the whole system on a whiteboard: the path of the air and the muscles that move it.

beats.scene: Iris sleeps under a blanket while a glowing dot in her head pulses
beats.summary: Iris asks how she keeps breathing when asleep, and Dev explains that the brainstem runs breathing automatically.

beats.scene: A hand with a steering wheel above a dial with a heartbeat line
beats.summary: Breathing is automatic, but unlike the heartbeat we can also take control of it.

beats.scene: A chart shows a rising line of carbon dioxide beside a small gasping face
beats.summary: The urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide, not by falling oxygen.

beats.scene: Iris holds her breath beside a clock with her cheeks puffed
beats.summary: Dev lets Iris hold her breath briefly to feel the urge build, and explains that this is safe in the air for a short time.

beats.scene: A swimming pool with a lifeguard on a chair and a clear warning sign
beats.summary: Dev warns that holding the breath in water, especially after breathing fast, can be dangerous, so never do it alone.

beats.scene: A clock beside a calm figure whose chest rises gently
beats.summary: At rest, most adults breathe about twelve to twenty times a minute, and Iris's count of sixteen is normal.

beats.scene: Four faces show laughing, gasping, sighing and crying with different breath shapes
beats.summary: Breathing changes with emotion: laughs, gasps, sighs and sobs are all kinds of breath.

beats.scene: A long sigh drawn as two short waves and one long wave
beats.summary: We sigh now and then, and one idea is that a sigh helps to reopen tiny air sacs, though this is not settled.

beats.scene: Iris talks in the hall while small arrows show breaths between her phrases
beats.summary: Speech uses the out-breath, so we take quick breaths between phrases without noticing.

beats.scene: A hand on a steering wheel beside a calm resting chest
beats.summary: Dev sums up: breathing is an autopilot we can also steer, and that gives Iris a way to practise.

beats.scene: A large drawing of a nose with arrows of air curling inside it
beats.summary: Dev says the nose is more than a place for glasses and smells: it is a built-in air conditioner.

beats.scene: A nose with soft arrows of warm air and tiny hairs drawn inside
beats.summary: The nose filters, warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs.

beats.scene: Tiny hairs and sticky mucus catch dust specks while small brushes sweep them away
beats.summary: Hairs, sticky mucus and tiny brush-like cilia trap dust and germs and sweep them out.

beats.scene: A face with a runny nose in the cold beside a small glowing sun
beats.summary: Dev explains that a runny nose in cold air is normal, because the nose makes more mucus to protect itself.

beats.scene: A face with the left nostril glowing at noon and the right at night
beats.summary: The nasal cycle: one side of the nose is more open than the other, and they swap every few hours.

beats.scene: A nostril glows softly with a small gas cloud drifting inside
beats.summary: The nose and sinuses make nitric oxide, which may help the lungs, though the evidence is still developing.

beats.scene: A bowl of steaming tea beside a nose and drifting scent curls
beats.summary: Breathing also carries smells to the roof of the nose, where sensors pass the news to the brain.

beats.scene: A person sits breathing through an open mouth after running a hill
beats.summary: Mouth breathing is normal during hard exercise or when the nose is blocked.

beats.scene: A sleeper with an open mouth beside a glass of water
beats.summary: Breathing through a dry mouth at night can mean a blocked nose or snoring, and a doctor can help.

beats.scene: Iris shows Dev a notebook full of small tally marks and sketches of noses
beats.summary: A few days on, Iris shows Dev her notebook of noticed breaths, and Dev says she has learned the machine.

beats.scene: Iris touches the top of her chest while Dev watches with a pen raised
beats.summary: Dev asks Iris where she feels her breath, and she points to the top of her chest.

beats.scene: A figure frozen in alarm, with a racing heart and heaving chest
beats.summary: Anxious breathing is often quick and high; it is part of the body's natural alarm, which helps in danger but not before a concert.

beats.scene: Iris sits with one hand on her chest and one on her belly
beats.summary: Dev shows Iris a simple exercise: one hand on the chest, one on the belly, to see which one moves more.

beats.scene: A belly gently widening below a calm hand as arrows of air flow down
beats.summary: Dev asks her to let the belly move gently on the in-breath, without pushing it out.

beats.scene: Two arrows, one on the chest and one on the belly, both pointing outward
beats.summary: Dev is honest: both the chest and belly move in a natural breath, and there is no single right way.

beats.scene: Iris lies on a floor with a book rising on her belly
beats.summary: At home, Iris practises lying on the floor with a book on her belly for five minutes.

beats.scene: A woman on a bus holds in her stomach under a coat
beats.summary: On a bus, Iris notices she holds her stomach in all the time, which stops the belly from moving.

beats.scene: Iris stands in the second row as Mara raises her baton
beats.summary: At rehearsal, Iris tries the low breath before the first note and feels it work for a moment.

beats.scene: A long staircase of musical notes with a small climbing figure on the steps
beats.summary: Dev says a new breathing habit needs repetition, like scales, and old habits come back for a while.

beats.scene: A calendar with two small ticks every day and a heart of gentle rings
beats.summary: Dev's homework: five quiet minutes twice a day, no forcing, and a note to see a doctor about unexplained breathlessness.

beats.scene: A clock with a slow gentle wave drawn across its face
beats.summary: Dev asks what happens if the breath is made slower, and says studies have looked at about six breaths a minute.

beats.scene: Iris sits with a timer beside four dots and six dots
beats.summary: Iris tries breathing in for four counts and out for six, which makes about six breaths a minute.

beats.scene: A heart line rises on an in-breath and falls on an out-breath
beats.summary: Iris feels her pulse and notices that the heart speeds up when she breathes in and slows when she breathes out.

beats.scene: A long nerve drawn as a thin line from the brain to the heart
beats.summary: Part of the reason is the vagus nerve, which can slow the heart, but how much it matters is still being studied.

beats.scene: A ribbon unrolls from a slow out-breath beside a resting heart
beats.summary: A longer out-breath may help the body to relax, though the evidence is modest.

beats.scene: A scale holds a stack of small studies and a question mark
beats.summary: Small studies suggest slow breathing may reduce stress scores or blood pressure a little, but many are short and the results vary.

beats.scene: A cartoon nerve wearing a cape beside a crossed-out sign saying hack your body
beats.summary: Dev warns that online claims about the vagus nerve are often stronger than the science.

beats.scene: Iris's notebook open to a page of small ticks, faces and notes
beats.summary: Iris keeps a diary of her slow-breathing practice and sees small changes: some days she feels calmer, others she feels nothing.

beats.scene: Mara smiles at Iris in the second row while the choir rests
beats.summary: Mara notices that Iris looks calmer at rehearsal, but the long phrase still gives Iris trouble.

beats.scene: A slow gentle wave above a heart with a smaller question mark beside it
beats.summary: Dev sums up: slow breathing is a gentle tool, six a minute is not magic, and she should pick a pace that feels comfortable.

beats.scene: Iris and Dev sit on a park bench under falling autumn leaves
beats.summary: Dev and Iris meet on a bench in the Park, where Iris tells him about a time she felt dizzy and tingly.

beats.scene: A scale tips as a cloud of exhaled arrows outweighs a small blue dot
beats.summary: Hyperventilation means breathing more than the body needs, which blows off too much carbon dioxide.

beats.scene: A woman breathes fast with tingling fingers and a dizzy swirl above her head
beats.summary: Too little carbon dioxide can narrow blood vessels in the brain and cause dizziness, tingling and a strange feeling.

beats.scene: A gasping face with a hand on the chest
beats.summary: People who breathe too fast often feel they cannot get enough air, which makes them breathe even faster.

beats.scene: A tangled thread loosens into a line beside a calm hand
beats.summary: Fast breathing is common in panic, and while a panic attack is not usually dangerous in itself, frequent attacks should be seen by a doctor.

beats.scene: A paper bag with a crossed-out circle drawn over it
beats.summary: Dev says breathing into a paper bag is no longer recommended, because it can be risky.

beats.scene: A hand on a knee, a slow arrow outward, and a calm bench
beats.summary: In the moment, slowing the out-breath and sitting down can help; if the feeling is new or there is chest pain, get medical help.

beats.scene: Iris stands in the concert hall wings breathing slowly with her eyes closed
beats.summary: Before rehearsal, Iris tries slow breathing in the wings and feels steadier, though not cured.

beats.scene: Sam the tenor grins at Iris in a corridor, a folder under his arm
beats.summary: Sam, a tenor in the choir, tells Iris that everyone is nervous before a concert and that he has a trick of his own.

beats.scene: A bench in the park at dusk with two figures and a long shadow
beats.summary: Dev says Iris is not fixing a fault but building a skill, and that the concert is four weeks away.

beats.scene: Dev draws a square on the whiteboard with a number beside each side
beats.summary: Dev draws a square on the whiteboard to teach box breathing: in, hold, out, hold, each for the same count.

beats.scene: Iris sits upright and traces a square in the air with one finger
beats.summary: Iris tries box breathing, and the holds feel odd, so she shortens the count to three.

beats.scene: A square of four equal arrows with a small thinking face in the middle
beats.summary: Some people find the equal counts steadying because counting gives the mind a simple job, but there is no proof that the box beats other slow patterns.

beats.scene: A crossed-out clock beside a smooth wave with no pauses
beats.summary: Iris does not like the holds, so Dev says she can skip them and breathe slowly in and out.

beats.scene: A long breath out follows two short breaths in, drawn as three small waves
beats.summary: Dev teaches cyclic sighing: a full breath in, a short extra breath in on top, and then a long, slow breath out.

beats.scene: A small scale holds a trial paper with a modest star beside it
beats.summary: One trial found five minutes a day of cyclic sighing lifted mood a little more than another method, but more studies are needed.

beats.scene: Iris sits on her bed at night, breathing in twice and out once
beats.summary: Iris tries cyclic sighing at home and enjoys the long out-breath, which feels like a proper sigh.

beats.scene: A hand holds a toolbox with three different shapes inside it
beats.summary: Dev says no pattern is magic; the best one is the one you can do and repeat, and patterns are just scaffolding for attention.

beats.scene: A warning triangle stands beside a crossed-out picture of fast heaving breath
beats.summary: Dev's safety rules: stop if dizzy, and ask a doctor first if you have a heart or lung condition or are pregnant.

beats.scene: Iris writes three small headings in her notebook beside a small lantern
beats.summary: Iris lists her three tools in her notebook: slow out-breath, low breath, and the sigh.

beats.scene: Sam holds out a phone showing a loud video with big bright words
beats.summary: Sam shows Iris an online video that promises one breathing trick will fix everything, and she takes it to Dev.

beats.scene: A ladder with three rungs labelled strong, modest and weak
beats.summary: Dev draws a ladder of evidence with three rungs: strong, modest and weak, and places each claim on it.

beats.scene: A body outline with a large lung and small liver and kidneys beside it
beats.summary: Dev says breathing mostly removes carbon dioxide, so claims that breathing detoxes the whole body are not supported.

beats.scene: A blood cell almost full of blue dots beside a large puffing face
beats.summary: In a healthy person at rest, the blood is already nearly full of oxygen, so breathing harder does not add much.

beats.scene: A pill bottle beside a calm figure breathing slowly
beats.summary: Dev says no breathing technique cures serious diseases, and people should never stop medicines because of a video.

beats.scene: A swimmer shape fainting beside a crossed-out clock and a steering wheel
beats.summary: Dev is wary of methods with fast breathing followed by long breath-holds, because people have fainted, so never do them in water or while driving.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over a page with four small question marks
beats.summary: Dev gives Iris four questions for any claim: who says it, how many people were studied, compared with what, and who profits.

beats.scene: Dev and Iris stand beside a small scale tipped slightly toward a gentle wave
beats.summary: Dev says that modest does not mean useless: slow breathing has real, if limited, support, and honesty cuts both ways.

beats.scene: Iris stands in the choir looking steady as Mara conducts the long phrase
beats.summary: At rehearsal, Iris nearly reaches the end of the long phrase of Snow Light, losing her breath only on the last word.

beats.scene: Dev and Iris walk out of the hall under a bright moon
beats.summary: At the halfway point, Dev says that the machinery is solid and the uses are modest, and that three weeks remain.

beats.scene: A choir stands in rows with open mouths while a conductor raises her hands
beats.summary: Mara invites Dev to join a rehearsal and explain breathing to the choir, since singers need long, controlled out-breaths.

beats.scene: A throat drawn as a tube with two folds vibrating like strings
beats.summary: Dev explains that sound begins when air passes the vocal folds in the larynx and makes them vibrate.

beats.scene: A row of ribs staying wide while a small belly slowly softens
beats.summary: Singers manage a long note by letting the ribs stay wide and the out-breath leave slowly, which voice teachers call support.

beats.scene: A singer takes a quick low breath through an open mouth between two phrases
beats.summary: Singers take quick, low breaths through the mouth and nose between phrases, a bit like a gentle surprise.

beats.scene: Choir members make bubbling sounds with their lips as a conductor laughs
beats.summary: Mara leads a warm-up of lip trills, a bubbling sound that makes the breath steady, and Iris collapses into giggles.

beats.scene: A stopwatch beside a long wavy line and a small friendly warning sign
beats.summary: Mara asks the choir to sustain a quiet hissing sound and time it; Iris reaches fourteen seconds, and Dev says numbers do not matter.

beats.scene: A score with small pencil commas between the notes and arrows above them
beats.summary: Mara tells singers to pencil commas where they will breathe, and explains that in a choir not everyone breathes at the same time.

beats.scene: Iris pencils a comma in the middle of the long phrase of Snow Light
beats.summary: Iris realises that she can take a quiet stolen breath in the long phrase of Snow Light, and that it was never meant for one breath.

beats.scene: Singers stand in a circle, each with a hand on a neighbour's back
beats.summary: Dev says singing in a group is enjoyed by many people and some small studies suggest a boost to well-being, but the evidence is modest.

beats.scene: A glass of water on a piano beside a small sign saying rest
beats.summary: Dev reminds the singers to drink water and rest the voice, and warns that hoarseness that lasts needs a doctor.

beats.scene: Iris hums with her fingertips on her nose in the quiet rehearsal room
beats.summary: Dev tells Iris to hum with her fingertips on her nose and feel the buzz.

beats.scene: A long breath out carries a hum, drawn as a wavy ribbon
beats.summary: A hum is a long out-breath with sound, so it slows the breath without needing a count.

beats.scene: A small gas cloud drifts in a nostril while a hum ripples
beats.summary: Dev says a small study found humming raised nitric oxide in the nose much more than quiet breathing, but what that means for health is not clear.

beats.scene: Iris hums a lullaby in a kitchen with her grandmother's old teapot beside her
beats.summary: Iris hums her grandmother's lullaby, and her breath slows without counting.

beats.scene: A comfortable figure sits on a stool as a long wave leaves its mouth
beats.summary: Dev gives Iris a simple routine: breathe in gently through the nose for four, then hum out for as long as is comfortable.

beats.scene: A woman at a bus stop humming with a small curious dog looking up
beats.summary: Iris hums quietly at a bus stop, and a curious dog and a smiling stranger notice.

beats.scene: A singer with hands near her cheeks feels a buzz in her face
beats.summary: Mara uses humming as a voice warm-up; the buzz in the front of the face helps singers find a forward, easy sound.

beats.scene: A nose with a caution sign over a hollow sinus space
beats.summary: Dev warns that humming is not a treatment for sinus problems, and anyone with pain should see a doctor.

beats.scene: Sam hums a deep note and a row of singers laughs
beats.summary: Iris teaches Sam to hum, and he produces a deep note that makes the whole row of singers laugh and join in.

beats.scene: A calendar with the concert date circled and two weeks crossed off
beats.summary: Two weeks before the concert, Iris notices that she is less afraid, and Dev says that is the practice working in small steps.

beats.scene: A slumped figure sits at a desk, then sits tall beside a bright window
beats.summary: Dev notices that Iris slumps in her chair, and asks whether posture changes how she breathes.

beats.scene: A folded figure with a squeezed chest and arrows struggling to widen the ribs
beats.summary: A slumped posture can limit how freely the ribs and diaphragm move, and some studies find small differences in lung function.

beats.scene: A figure sits upright as a thread gently lifts her head
beats.summary: Sitting tall helps a little, but not by stiffening: Dev suggests imagining a thread lifting the top of the head.

beats.scene: A desk with a note saying breathe and a ticking timer
beats.summary: At her desk, Iris sets a reminder to sit tall and breathe, but her slump keeps returning, and Dev says to be kind to herself.

beats.scene: A row of small figures in different positions from standing to stretching
beats.summary: Dev says the best posture is the next one: moving often matters more than holding a perfect position.

beats.scene: A figure stands with one arm raised over her head and leans gently sideways
beats.summary: Dev shows a gentle side stretch: raise one arm, lean over, and feel the ribs on the other side widen as she breathes.

beats.scene: Shoulders roll backward and drop down while a neck softens with a gentle curve
beats.summary: Iris learns to roll her shoulders back and down and to soften her neck, which eases the tension that rises when she is nervous.

beats.scene: Singers stand on risers with soft knees and relaxed feet shoulder-width apart
beats.summary: Mara tells singers to stand with feet apart and knees soft, since locked knees can make people faint on stage.

beats.scene: A person looks down at a phone, then holds it up
beats.summary: Dev says that looking down at a phone for hours can round the shoulders; holding it higher and taking breaks may help a little.

beats.scene: Dev and Iris stand side by side in a bright window
beats.summary: Dev says posture is a helper, not a cure, and Iris should not worry about getting it perfect.

beats.scene: Iris and Dev walk fast up a park hill in the cold
beats.summary: On a cold Saturday, Dev takes Iris for a fast walk up a hill in the Park to watch breathing change with exercise.

beats.scene: A leg muscle glows as arrows of oxygen rush in
beats.summary: Working muscles use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide, and the brain notices and speeds up breathing.

beats.scene: Two arrows grow longer and more frequent as a figure climbs a steep slope
beats.summary: In exercise we breathe both faster and deeper, so the amount of air moved each minute can rise many times above its resting level.

beats.scene: A walker and a talker with a speech bubble, and a gasping figure
beats.summary: Dev teaches the talk test: if you can talk but not sing, the effort is moderate; if you can only gasp, slow down.

beats.scene: A hill path with a figure taking deep breaths through an open mouth
beats.summary: On the steep part of the hill Iris breathes through her mouth and Dev says that is perfectly normal.

beats.scene: Two figures breathe out white clouds on a frosty hill
beats.summary: Iris sees her breath in the cold, which Dev explains is water vapour condensing in cold air.

beats.scene: A person pulls a scarf over the nose and mouth in wind
beats.summary: Cold air can make some people cough or wheeze, and a scarf over the mouth warms the air; a doctor should check wheeze or tightness during exercise.

beats.scene: A figure running comfortably beside a chart with a gently rising line
beats.summary: Regular exercise helps the heart and lungs work better, so the same effort feels easier over weeks; this is high on the evidence ladder.

beats.scene: Iris sits on a hilltop bench as her breath slows
beats.summary: After the climb, Iris sits on a bench while her breath and heart slow; Dev says how quickly they settle is one sign of fitness.

beats.scene: Iris stands on the hilltop humming a long note with the city spread below
beats.summary: On the hilltop, Iris hums a long note, finds it longer and steadier than before, and counts twelve days to the concert.

beats.scene: Dev holds a framed photo of a snowy mountain pass
beats.summary: Dev shows Iris a photo of a mountain pass where he once walked, and tells her how breathless he felt there.

beats.scene: A mountain drawn with fewer dots of air around a hiker near the top
beats.summary: At altitude the mix of gases is the same, but the air pressure is lower, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules.

beats.scene: A tall peak with a small flag and a hiker breathing hard
beats.summary: On the very highest mountains, the air pressure is only about a third of that at sea level, so each breath contains about a third of the oxygen.

beats.scene: A hiker's chest widening with fast deep arrows while a heart beats quicker
beats.summary: At altitude the body responds at once: breathing becomes faster and deeper, and the heart beats faster.

beats.scene: A calendar with several days on a mountain and a body slowly changing colour
beats.summary: Over days and weeks the body adapts, making more red blood cells and adjusting its breathing, so going up slowly gives time to adapt.

beats.scene: A hiker sits on a rock holding his aching head
beats.summary: Dev warns that mountain sickness can cause headaches, nausea and tiredness; if it gets worse, go down and get medical help.

beats.scene: Small village homes with smoke from chimneys on a high mountain plateau

beats.scene: Iris stands at a window with a mug, looking at distant hills
beats.summary: Iris reflects that breathing depends on the air and the place around her, and that she no longer takes it for granted.

beats.scene: A person with a hand on the chest beside a cloud of grey haze

B1B2: Iris sings in a choir, and tonight is the first rehearsal of the Winter Concert. Her heart is racing, and she notices that she is taking quick, shallow breaths high in her chest.
Mara, the choir director, claps her hands and tells everyone that the Winter Concert is only six weeks away. The last song, Snow Light, is beautiful, she says, but it has one very long phrase.
The choir sings Snow Light for the first time, and Iris reaches the long phrase with a head full of worry. Halfway through it, her breath runs out, and she has to stop and gasp.
Dev, her friend, works as a respiratory physiotherapist, which means that he helps people to breathe more easily. He notices her fast breathing and says that it is something that can be understood.

Dev suggests that they meet twice a week until the concert and explore how breathing really works. He promises to be honest, and to say clearly when something is proved and when it is only a hopeful idea.
Dev starts with a surprising number that makes Iris stare. A person takes roughly twenty thousand breaths in a day, and most of them happen without a single thought.
Dev asks her to watch the clock and count every breath she takes in one minute. She counts sixteen, and she is surprised that it is neither as fast nor as slow as she had thought.
The body's cells burn fuel to make energy, and they need oxygen to do it. Dev says it is rather like a fire, which cannot burn without a steady supply of air.
Burning fuel makes a waste gas called carbon dioxide, and breathing carries it away. Dev draws two arrows on a whiteboard, one pointing in and one pointing out.

Dev gives Iris a small task for the week: she must notice her breathing three times a day without trying to change it. She walks home under the streetlights, feeling her breath go in and out, and for once she does not mind it.
Two days later, Iris visits Dev's clinic, where a plastic model of the lungs sits on his desk. He says that the best way to understand a breath is to follow it on its journey.
Air enters through the nose or the mouth and passes down the throat. Then it reaches a tube called the windpipe, which carries it toward the lungs.
A small flap of tissue called the epiglottis closes over the windpipe whenever we swallow. That is why food goes to the stomach, although it sometimes goes the wrong way, and then we cough.
The windpipe is held open by firm rings of cartilage, which are shaped like the letter C. Dev tells Iris to touch the front of her neck, and she feels the hard rings under her skin.
Low in the chest, the windpipe divides into two tubes called bronchi, one for each lung. The left lung is a little smaller than the right one, because it has to make room for the heart.

The two bronchi keep dividing into smaller and smaller tubes, like a tree turned upside down. Dev says that nobody has found a better description, and Iris admits that it makes her lungs sound like a garden.
At the end of the smallest tubes are tiny air sacs called alveoli. Each lung has hundreds of millions of them, and together they give the lungs a surface far larger than they seem.

The walls of the air sacs are thinner than a hair, and they are wrapped in tiny blood vessels called capillaries. Oxygen passes through the wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes the other way.
Inside the red blood cells is a substance called haemoglobin, which holds on to oxygen. It contains iron, and that is what gives blood its red colour.
The heart pumps the blood from the lungs to every part of the body. A full circuit takes roughly a minute at rest, so one breath of air quickly becomes energy in a muscle.

Dev holds up a soft sponge and asks Iris what makes the lungs pull air in. She guesses that the lungs do it themselves, but he explains that they are more like sponges and have no muscles of their own.
The diaphragm is a large, dome-shaped muscle that sits beneath the lungs, like a parachute under a ribcage. When it tightens, it flattens and moves down, and air is drawn into the lungs.
When the diaphragm moves down, the space inside the chest gets bigger, and the air pressure inside falls. Air from outside then flows in to fill the space, so we do not need to suck it in.

Dev makes a little model from a plastic bottle, a balloon and a rubber sheet that stretches across the bottom. When Iris pulls the rubber sheet down, the balloon inside fills with air, just like a lung.
When the diaphragm relaxes, it rises back into its dome shape, and the stretchy lungs spring back to their smaller size. At rest, breathing out takes almost no effort, and the air simply leaves.
Dev asks Iris to lie on a mat with a light book on her belly. When she breathes in slowly, the book rises, because the descending diaphragm gently pushes the organs below it outward.
The ribs and the muscles between them, called the intercostal muscles, also work as we breathe. They lift the ribs up and outward, rather like the handle of a bucket, and make the chest wider.
When breathing is hard or anxious, extra muscles in the neck and shoulders help to lift the chest. Iris notices that her own shoulders rise when she is nervous, and that her neck feels tight.

A hiccup is a sudden jerk of the diaphragm, followed by the vocal folds snapping shut, which makes the “hic” sound. Most hiccups stop by themselves, and doctors often do not know exactly why they start.
Dev draws the whole system on the whiteboard, from the nose to the diaphragm. Iris copies it into her notebook and writes one word under it: partners.
Iris asks Dev how she keeps breathing while she is asleep. He explains that a part of the brain called the brainstem sets the rhythm all night, without any help from her.
Breathing runs on autopilot, but unlike the heartbeat, we can also take over and steer it. We do this when we talk, sing, sigh, hold our breath or blow out a candle.
Many people think that we breathe because oxygen runs low, but this is not quite right. The strong urge to take a breath comes mainly from rising carbon dioxide in the blood.
Dev asks Iris to hold her breath for a short moment and notice what she feels. The urge to breathe grows quickly, and he explains that for a healthy person a short breath-hold in the air is safe.
Dev gives a serious warning about holding the breath in water. People have fainted and drowned by breathing fast and then holding their breath, so it should never be practised alone or in water.
At rest, most adults breathe about twelve to twenty times a minute. Iris's sixteen was right in the middle, so there was nothing wrong with her breathing rate when she was calm.
Emotions change the way that we breathe, every day. A laugh, a gasp, a sigh and a sob are all patterns of breath, and each one has its own rhythm.
We all sigh now and then, even when we do not feel sad. One idea is that a sigh helps to reopen some of the tiny air sacs, although scientists have not settled the question.
When we talk, we use the out-breath to make sound, and we take quick breaths between phrases without noticing. Iris listens to herself, and she hears how often she snatches a breath.
Dev sums up the lesson of the evening: breathing is an autopilot that we can also steer. This is a gift, because it means Iris can practise, and she decides to start with small steps.
Dev asks Iris why people have a nose, and she says it is for smelling. He agrees, but adds that the nose is also a small air conditioner for everything we breathe.
The nose filters the air, warms it and moistens it before it reaches the lungs. Cold, dry air would irritate the lungs, so the nose prepares it on the way in.
Hairs just inside the nostrils catch the larger specks of dust. Further in, a layer of sticky mucus traps smaller ones, and tiny brush-like cilia sweep it all away.
Iris says that her nose always runs in the cold, and she wonders if something is wrong. Dev says it is normal, because the nose makes extra mucus to warm and protect the air.
Dev tells Iris to close one nostril and breathe in, and then to try the other. One side is usually more open, because the nose follows a cycle that swaps sides every few hours.
The nose and the sinuses make a gas called nitric oxide. Scientists think it may help to fight germs and to widen blood vessels in the lungs, although the evidence is still developing.
The air that we breathe also carries smells to the nose. Tiny scent particles reach sensors in the roof of the nose, and they send a message to the brain, which often brings back memories.

Iris asks whether it is wrong to breathe through the mouth, since she once read that it is. Dev says no, because during hard exercise the mouth lets in more air, even though it filters and warms it less.
Dev adds a note of caution about the night. If someone often wakes with a dry mouth, the nose may be blocked or they may snore, so a doctor can help.
A week after the first rehearsal, Iris shows Dev her notebook of noticed breaths. Her breath goes high and fast whenever she hurries, and Dev tells her that she now knows the machine.
Dev asks Iris to show him where she feels her breath move when she is worried. She points to the top of her chest, close to her collarbones.
When we are afraid, the body releases adrenaline, and breathing gets faster and higher in the chest. This alarm is useful when there is real danger, but it is less helpful before a concert.

On a cool afternoon, Iris and Dev sit on a bench in the park. She tells him about a time on a station platform when she felt dizzy and her fingers began to tingle.

As the light fades, Dev tells Iris that she is not fixing a fault but building a skill. The concert is only four weeks away, but there is still time to practise.

Dev explains that a hum is simply a long, gentle out-breath with sound on it. It slows the breath down naturally, without needing any counting at all.

At home, Iris hums a lullaby that her grandmother used to sing. Her breath slows without any counting at all, and a quiet warmth spreads across her chest.
Dev suggests a simple routine that Iris can repeat a few times a day. She breathes in gently through the nose for four counts, then hums out for as long as is comfortable.
Iris tries humming very quietly at a bus stop on a cold morning. A dog looks up at her with interest, and a stranger smiles, and she realises that nobody minds at all.
Mara starts the next rehearsal with a humming warm-up. She says that the buzz at the front of the face helps singers to find an easy, forward sound before they open their mouths.
Dev adds a warning about humming and the nose. Some people say that humming can treat sinus problems, but this is not proved, so anyone with pain in the face should see a doctor.
Iris shows Sam the humming routine in the corridor. He hums a very deep note, the row of singers joins in, and soon the corridor is full of a warm, buzzing laughter.
Two weeks before the concert, Iris notices that she feels less afraid than she did. Dev says that this is how practice works, in small steps that are easy to miss.
In the clinic, Dev notices that Iris slumps down in her chair, with her shoulders rounded. He asks her if she thinks that the way we sit can change the way we breathe.

At work, Iris puts a note on her desk and sets a gentle reminder on her phone. Her slump keeps coming back, but Dev tells her to be kind to herself and simply start again.
Dev tells Iris that no single posture is perfect. The best one is the next one, because moving often matters more than holding any position for hours.
Dev shows Iris a gentle side stretch that she can do at a desk. She raises one arm and leans to the side, and she feels the ribs on the other side open as she breathes in.
Iris learns to roll her shoulders slowly back and down, and to let her neck relax. This eases the tension that rises into her shoulders whenever she is nervous.
Mara tells the choir to stand with their feet a little apart and their knees soft. She says that locked knees can make a person feel faint after standing still for a long time.
Dev says that looking down at a phone for hours can round the shoulders and bend the neck. Holding the phone a little higher and taking breaks may help, although the research on this is modest.
Dev sums up the lesson of the day: good posture is a helper, not a cure. Iris should not worry about getting it perfect, because a relaxed, moving body is the real goal.
On a cold Saturday, Dev takes Iris to the Park for a brisk walk up the biggest hill. He says that the best way to understand exercise breathing is to feel it.
When the muscles work hard, they use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. The brain notices this, and it tells the diaphragm and ribs to work faster and harder.
During exercise, breathing gets both faster and deeper at the same time. In hard exercise, the amount of air that moves in and out in a minute can rise many times above its resting level.
Dev teaches Iris a simple method called the talk test. If she can talk but not sing, the effort is about right for most people, and if she can only gasp, she should slow down.
On the steepest part of the hill, Iris finds that she is breathing through her mouth. She worries a little, but Dev says that it is perfectly normal during hard exercise.
In the cold air, Iris can see her breath as little white clouds. Dev explains that the breath is warm and full of water vapour, and the vapour turns into tiny drops in the cold.
Dev says that cold air makes some people cough or wheeze. A scarf over the mouth warms the air a little, but chest tightness or wheeze during exercise is something to ask a doctor about.
Dev explains that regular exercise helps the heart and lungs work better. Over a few weeks, the same effort feels easier, and this is one claim that sits high on the evidence ladder.
At the top, Iris sits on a bench and feels her breath and her heart slow down. Dev says that how quickly they settle is one small sign of fitness.
On the hilltop, Iris hums a long note and finds that it is steadier than a month ago. Dev tells her that there are only twelve days left until the Winter Concert.
In the clinic, Dev shows Iris a photograph of a high mountain pass where he once walked on holiday. He tells her that he felt strangely breathless there, even though he was fit.
Dev explains that the air on a mountain has the same mix of gases as at sea level. But the air pressure is lower, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules.
On the highest mountains in the world, the air pressure is only about a third of that at sea level. Each breath there carries only about a third of the oxygen.
When people climb high, the body responds straight away. Breathing becomes faster and deeper, and the heart beats a little faster to move the oxygen around.
Over days and weeks, the body adapts to thin air by adjusting its breathing and by making more red blood cells. This is called acclimatisation, and it is why people should climb slowly.

Dev adds a serious warning about mountain sickness, which people can get on high mountains. It can cause headaches and a sick feeling, and if it gets worse, the answer is to go down and get medical help.
Some groups of people have lived high in the mountains for many generations. Scientists have found that their bodies have differences that help them to live well in thin air.
Iris asks whether special training masks or altitude tents are worth buying. Dev says that the evidence is mixed, and that most people do not need them at all.

On an aeroplane the cabin pressure is lower than at sea level, a little like being on a modest mountain. Most healthy people do not notice, but people with lung problems should ask a doctor before flying.
That evening, Iris looks out of her window at the distant hills. She thinks that her breath depends on the air and the place around her, and she no longer takes it for granted.
On a hazy morning, Dev meets Iris at the clinic window and points to the grey sky. He tells her that the quality of the air matters as much as the way we breathe it.
Dev explains that very fine particles from traffic, smoke and fires can travel deep into the lungs. The body's defences catch many of them, but they cannot catch them all.
Polluted air can irritate the airways, and it can make asthma and some heart conditions worse. Studies have also linked long-term exposure to a higher risk of health problems.
Dev says that the air inside our homes matters too. Opening a window, using a fan when cooking and keeping damp rooms dry can all help, because mould can irritate the airways of some people.
Dev suggests that, when it is possible, people should walk or exercise away from busy roads. On days when the air is bad, an air quality report can help them to choose their plans.
Dev explains that cigarette smoke damages the tiny cilia and irritates the airways. Iris thinks of her uncle Tom, who smoked for forty years and was often short of breath.
Dev says that stopping smoking helps at any age. Iris's uncle Tom stopped at sixty, and he says that stairs feel easier now, and that he coughs a lot less.
Dev says that health services offer help for people who want to stop smoking, such as advice, medicines and telephone support. Many people try more than once, and that is not failure.
Dev mentions vaping, which is much newer than smoking. Researchers are still learning about its long-term effects, and it is not harmless, so people who do not smoke should not start.
That evening, Iris phones her uncle Tom and invites him to the Winter Concert. He is delighted and promises to come, and there are only ten days to go.
In the corridor before rehearsal, Sam takes out a small inhaler and uses it. He tells Iris that he has asthma, and she realises that she never knew.
In asthma, the walls of the airways are sore and swollen, and the muscles around them can tighten. This makes the tubes narrow, and it causes wheeze, cough and a tight chest.
Asthma is managed with a plan from a doctor. Many people have a reliever inhaler for symptoms, and some also use a daily preventer, and Sam follows his plan carefully.

Dev says that breathing exercises may help some people with asthma to feel better as an extra. The evidence is modest, and the inhaler plan from a doctor always comes first.
Dev gives a very clear and serious warning about asthma. Someone who is severely breathless, who cannot speak in full sentences or whose inhaler is not helping needs emergency help at once.

Dev says that many people do not use their inhalers quite correctly. It is well worth asking a pharmacist or a nurse to check, because good technique means that more of the medicine reaches the lungs.
Iris gives a cough in the middle of a sentence and apologises. Dev says that there is no need, because a cough is a useful defence that blows irritants out of the airways.
Dev says that most coughs after a cold fade within a few weeks. One that lasts about three weeks should be checked by a doctor, and so should a cough with blood in it.
Sam tells Iris that he is glad that she did not make a fuss about his asthma. They share a banana, laugh, and walk back to rehearsal, with a week to go before the concert.
With six days to go, Iris lies awake in the small hours, worrying about the concert. The next day she asks Dev what her breathing does while she sleeps.
Dev explains that breathing changes through the night in a regular way. It becomes slower and steadier in deep sleep, and it is more irregular when we are dreaming.
Dev says that slow, quiet breathing in bed may help some people to relax and fall asleep. The evidence is modest, but it costs nothing and is safe for most healthy people.
Dev adds that he is not a sleep expert. Simple habits like a regular bedtime help many people, but poor sleep that lasts for weeks is worth talking to a doctor about.
Dev explains that snoring happens when the throat muscles relax and the space gets narrower. The soft tissues then vibrate as air flows through, and it is common and often harmless.
Dev says that loud snoring with pauses in breathing may be a sign of sleep apnoea. People should not try to guess, because a doctor can test for it and can treat it.
Dev says that often it is a partner or a friend who notices the pauses in breathing, not the sleeper. Anyone who is told that they stop breathing in their sleep should see a doctor.
Dev warns about a popular trend of taping the mouth shut at night. There is little evidence that it helps, and it may be unsafe, so a blocked nose should be seen by a doctor instead.
Dev adds that for some people who snore, sleeping on their side instead of their back may help. The effect varies, and it is not a replacement for seeing a doctor if apnoea is suspected.
Iris asks why we yawn, and Dev admits that scientists are not sure. There are several ideas, including cooling the brain, but none of them has been proved.
In the waiting room, a newborn baby is crying, and Dev tells Iris about the very first breath. Before birth the lungs are filled with fluid, and the first cry helps to fill them with air.
Dev explains that babies and young children breathe much faster than adults. Their lungs and bodies are small, and the rate slowly falls as they grow.
The lungs grow through childhood and work best in early adulthood, in the twenties. After that, lung capacity slowly declines with age, in a gentle slope that most people never notice.

Dev says that staying active throughout life helps to keep breathing comfortable. Walking, singing, dancing and climbing stairs all count, and there is strong evidence for the benefits of being active.
Iris admires Edith, the oldest alto in the choir, who is eighty-one and sings long phrases on a steady breath. Dev says that anyone with new or worse breathlessness should see a doctor, at any age.
Dev says that the best habit is a small one. He suggests a few minutes of slow, gentle breathing a few times a day, for instance when she wakes, after lunch and before bed.
Dev and Iris write a simple plan for the day of the concert. It includes a morning walk, a hum in the wings and a low breath before the first note.
Mara asks Iris to lead the warm-up before the dress rehearsal. She is nervous, but she leads the lip trills and the humming, and the whole choir follows her.
At the dress rehearsal, Iris takes her low breath and sings the long phrase of Snow Light, with a quiet breath in the right place. Mara beams at her, and the whole choir smiles.
On the night before the concert, Dev tells Iris that she has not been fixed, because there was never a fault. She has learned a skill, and some fear before a concert is quite normal.
On the morning of the Winter Concert, Iris follows her plan and takes a gentle walk. She hums a little as she goes, and she watches her breath float away in the frosty air.
In the evening, the town hall begins to fill with people in warm coats. Iris peeks through the curtain and sees Tom waving his scarf, and Dev sitting in the front row.
Backstage, Iris feels the old signs begin: her heart races and her breath goes quick and high. This time she does not panic, because she knows what they are.
Iris uses her tools one after another, as she has practised. She breathes in for four counts and out for six, and she hums softly while Sam grins and Edith squeezes her hand.
The choir files onto the stage under the bright lamps, and the audience grows quiet. Iris stands in the second row with soft knees and her shoulders down.
The first songs go well, and Iris notices that her breath is rising and falling in an easy rhythm. The music seems to carry her along, and she even enjoys herself.
Then comes Snow Light, the last song, with its long phrase. Iris takes a low breath, sings the first half and takes her quiet breath in the place that she has marked.
The last chord fades into the hall, and for a moment nobody moves. Then the audience rises and begins to clap, and the sound goes on for a long time.
After the concert, Dev tells Iris over tea that breathing is a useful tool, but not a cure for everything. He says that the best thing she has gained is the habit of noticing her breath.

This book has given general information about breathing, and science is still learning more about it. It is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor if you have worries about your breathing or your health.

A small, nervous ripple passed along the rows, and Iris felt it settle in her own chest.

The choir began Snow Light, and Iris sang well until she reached the long phrase, where her breath, already thin with worry, simply gave out. Almost all of them happen without a moment of thought, in sleep and in conversation, in boredom and in fear, which makes breathing the most repeated action of our lives. Yet hardly anyone, he said, has ever been taught how to do it well.

When the minute was over she had counted sixteen, which seemed neither fast nor slow, and she realised that simply paying attention had changed the whole thing a little. Dev smiled and said that this is the first lesson, and that it is worth remembering.

Every cell in the body burns fuel to produce energy, and in most cases it needs oxygen to do so, rather like a fire that cannot burn without a steady supply of air. Dev explained that this burning is quiet and slow, a gentle glow rather than a flame, but that it never stops for a single second of our lives. Without a fresh supply of oxygen, he said, the cells would soon fall silent, which is exactly why the body takes breathing so seriously.

The burning creates a waste gas, carbon dioxide, which must be carried away, and breathing is the process that delivers one gas and removes the other. Dev drew two arrows on a whiteboard, one pointing in and one pointing out, and announced that everything else in the story was detail. Iris stared at the arrows and thought that it was strange how much of her life was balanced on something so simple.

Dev set her one small task for the first week, which was simply to notice her breathing three times a day without trying to improve it. Iris walked home through the cold evening with one hand on her stomach, feeling the air move in and out, and she was amused to find that it felt almost like greeting an old friend she had ignored for years. Somewhere between the hall and her front door, the hammering in her chest finally eased.

Iris sat down with her notebook, feeling oddly like a tourist about to visit her own body.

The throat is shared by air and by food, which makes it a rather busy junction, and Dev likened it to a crossroads where two roads meet for a few centimetres before parting. The windpipe, which doctors call the trachea, is held open by a stack of firm cartilage rings shaped like the letter C, so that it never collapses when we breathe in. It was a strange feeling to meet a part of herself that she had been carrying around for decades.

Dev pointed out that the two lungs are not quite the same, because the left one is a little smaller than the right to leave room for the heart tucked beside it. Iris laughed that her body had solved a packing problem long before she had ever heard of one.

These two bronchi split again and again, becoming narrower each time, until they form a structure like a tree turned upside down, with its twigs finishing in tiny hollow tips. The walls of the alveoli are extraordinarily thin, and they are wrapped in networks of the smallest blood vessels, the capillaries, so that gases can pass between air and blood with hardly any barrier in the way. Oxygen moves into the blood because there is more of it in the air sacs, while carbon dioxide travels the other way, and neither movement needs any effort from us. It is a quiet and elegant piece of physics, Dev said, which happens about twenty thousand times a day.

Inside every red blood cell there is a protein called haemoglobin, which grabs hold of oxygen in the lungs and releases it wherever the body needs it. It contains iron, and that metal is also what gives blood its deep red colour, as Dev reminded her with a smile. A single red cell, he added, makes the whole journey from lung to muscle and back again, over and over, for about four months.

Once the blood has picked up its oxygen, the heart pumps it out to every part of the body, from the brain to the tips of the toes.
