Dev put the model down and said that, for now, he wanted her to remember only that breathing and the heart are partners.

Dev held up a soft sponge and asked Iris what pulled the air into her lungs, and she guessed, naturally enough, that the lungs did it themselves. He shook his head and explained that the lungs are spongy and elastic but have no muscles of their own, so they cannot move without help. Something else must do the pulling, he said, and it was the most hard-working muscle she owned.

The diaphragm is a broad, dome-shaped muscle that stretches beneath the lungs like a parachute stretched across the bottom of the ribcage. When it contracts it flattens and moves downwards, making more room in the chest and drawing air in through the nose and mouth. Dev said that this one muscle does most of the work of an ordinary quiet breath, which is a remarkable amount for something so rarely noticed.

When the diaphragm moves down, the space inside the chest gets bigger and the air pressure inside the lungs falls a little below the pressure outside. Air then flows in from the room to even things out, which means that we do not really pull air in at all, but make space and let it arrive. Iris found this oddly comforting, because it suggested that breathing is more about allowing than about effort.

Dev made a simple model from a plastic bottle with its base cut away, a balloon fixed inside the neck and a sheet of rubber stretched across the bottom. When Iris tugged the rubber downwards, the balloon swelled with air, and when she let go it shrank again, exactly as a lung does when the diaphragm moves. She tried it five times in a row, delighted, as if she had just been shown a magic trick with no secret.

When the diaphragm relaxes it drifts back up into its dome, and the elastic lungs spring back to their smaller size, pushing the air out as they go. At rest, then, the out-breath takes almost no effort at all, and it is only when we sing, shout or blow out candles that other muscles join in. Dev said that this is why the in-breath feels like an action and the out-breath feels like a sigh.

Dev asked Iris to lie on a mat with a light paperback resting on her belly, and to breathe in as slowly as she could manage. The book rose, which puzzled her until he explained that the descending diaphragm gently presses the organs beneath it outward, so the belly swells even though the air is going nowhere near it. She watched the paperback lift and fall like a small boat on a calm sea.

The ribs have a part to play as well, because the small intercostal muscles between them lift each rib up and outwards, a little like the handle of a bucket swinging up from its rim. This makes the chest wider from side to side as well as deeper from front to back, and the effect is easiest to see on a thin person in a quiet room. Dev asked Iris to put her hands on the sides of her ribs, and she felt them move like a gentle accordion.

When breathing is hard work, or when we are anxious, the muscles of the neck and shoulders join in to heave the upper chest upwards. Iris noticed that her own shoulders crept towards her ears whenever she thought about Snow Light, and that her neck felt tight as a violin string by the end of a rehearsal. These helpers are fine for emergencies, Dev said, but they are tiring when asked to do the job all day.

Dev mentioned, with a straight face, that the diaphragm is also responsible for hiccups, which are sudden involuntary jerks of the muscle followed by a quick snap of the vocal folds. That snap makes the familiar “hic” sound, and while some causes are known, such as eating too fast, the reason for many bouts is simply not clear. Most hiccups stop on their own, he said, and the many famous cures have never been properly proved.

By the end of the hour Dev had drawn the entire system on the whiteboard, from the nostrils down through the branching tubes to the sacs, with the dome of the diaphragm swinging beneath them. Iris copied it carefully into her notebook, adding arrows of her own, and then wrote the word partners at the bottom, because she had noticed that nothing in the diagram worked alone. Dev read it over her shoulder and said that this was the whole lesson in a single word.

Iris asked how on earth she managed to keep breathing through the night, when she was not around to remind herself. Dev explained that a region at the base of the brain, the brainstem, sets the rhythm of breathing and sends signals to the diaphragm all day and all night, without needing her thoughts or her permission. It is an old and sturdy piece of design, he said, and it has been working since the day she was born.

Breathing runs on autopilot, yet it is unusual among the body's automatic jobs because we can also take the wheel and steer. We do it whenever we talk, sing, sigh, gasp, whistle or blow out a candle, and then the control slips quietly back to the brainstem without our noticing. Dev said that this double life is exactly what makes breathing so interesting, and perhaps so useful.

Most people assume that the urge to breathe is a signal that oxygen is running low, but this is not quite right. The brain's sensors are far more sensitive to rising carbon dioxide, which makes the blood slightly more acidic, and it is that change which produces the strong urge to take a breath. Dev said that this is a clever design, because carbon dioxide gives an early and reliable warning.

Dev invited Iris to hold her breath for a short moment and to notice exactly how it felt. The urge to breathe grew quickly from a mild itch into a firm demand, and when she gave in and gasped, he told her that a short breath-hold in the air is safe for a healthy person. The urge will always win in the end, he said, though that does not mean she should try anything dramatic.

Dev's voice grew serious as he gave a warning about water, because people who breathe fast and then hold their breath in a pool can faint without any alarm from the body, and some have drowned. For this reason breath-holding should never be practised alone, in water or anywhere near it, he said, and even a lifeguard is no substitute for good sense. Iris wrote the warning in her notebook in capital letters and underlined it twice, just to be sure.

At rest, most healthy adults breathe about twelve to twenty times a minute, so Iris's count of sixteen from their first evening was perfectly ordinary. Children and babies breathe faster, he told her, and most people breathe a little more slowly in deep sleep, but there is no single perfect number. She was relieved to learn that she was not broken, and that the trouble began only when her breath sped up with her nerves.

Emotions are written in the breath, Dev told her, because a laugh, a gasp, a sigh and a sob are each a distinctive pattern of air moving in and out. A laugh is a string of short out-breaths, a gasp is a sharp in-breath, and a sob is a shuddering series of both. We recognise all of them in other people without ever being taught, and Dev added that the link between feelings and breath runs in both directions, which is why he finds it so interesting.

Everyone sighs from time to time, often without noticing, and not always because they are sad or tired or relieved. One idea, which Dev called plausible rather than proved, is that a deep sigh helps to reopen some of the tiny air sacs that have gone slightly flat, and another is that it resets the rhythm of breathing. Iris realised, rather happily, that she had been giving herself small free treatments for years.

When we speak, we borrow the out-breath to make sound, and in between our phrases we steal quick in-breaths so cleverly that the listener hardly notices. Dev asked Iris to describe her day aloud, and when she listened to herself, she was startled to find how often she snatched a little gasp of air between her sentences. Singing asks for something far more demanding, he said, and they would come to that.

Dev closed the notebook with a summary that fitted in a pocket, which was that breathing is an autopilot that we can also steer. It is the one automatic function of the body that gives us a handle, he said, and because it works both ways, a change in the breath can sometimes ripple into how we feel, though only up to a point. Iris decided that she would try steering a little, gently, and with plenty of patience.

Dev asked Iris why people have noses, and she answered, quite reasonably, that they are for smelling. He agreed that smell was part of it, but explained that the nose is also a built-in air conditioner, preparing every breath before it reaches the delicate lungs. She had always thought of her nose as something that held up her glasses and occasionally ran.

The nose filters the air, warms it and adds moisture, so that by the time a breath reaches the lungs it is much closer to body temperature and humidity. Cold, dry air can irritate the delicate tubes below, and Dev described the nasal passages as a winding corridor in which each breath is given a quick refit before the next stage of its trip. Iris admitted, with a smile, that she had never once thanked her nose for anything.

Coarse hairs just inside the nostrils catch the larger specks of dust, while further in, a thin layer of sticky mucus traps smaller particles and many of the germs that ride on them. Beneath the mucus, millions of microscopic hairs called cilia beat in waves, sweeping it all towards the throat, where it is swallowed and dealt with by the stomach. Iris laughed that this was the most polite cleaning system she had ever heard of.

Iris confessed that her nose always ran when she walked home in the cold, and she wondered whether it meant something was wrong. Dev reassured her that it was entirely normal, since the lining of the nose makes extra fluid to moisten and warm the cold, dry air, and sometimes it makes more than it can handle. A runny nose in winter, he said, is usually a sign of an efficient machine rather than a broken one.

Dev asked Iris to press one nostril closed and breathe in, then to try the other side, and she was astonished to find that one was clearly more open than its neighbour. This is the nasal cycle, he explained, in which the lining of each side swells and shrinks in turn, so that the work of breathing passes from one nostril to the other every few hours. It is a normal rhythm that most of us never notice, he added, until we catch a cold.

The nose and the air spaces behind it, the sinuses, produce a small amount of a gas called nitric oxide, which travels down with each breath. Researchers think that it may help to defend against germs and to widen the blood vessels in the lungs, but Dev was careful to add that this is still an active area of research. Nobody should treat it as a miracle, he said, and he promised to be honest each time they reached the place where the evidence stopped.

Breathing also carries scent through the nose, which is easy to forget, and it matters more than most people think. Tiny particles drift up to sensors in the roof of the nose, which send their messages straight to the brain and often summon memories more vividly than a photograph can. Dev put a cup of mint tea under Iris's nose, and she smiled, because the smell at once took her back to the kitchen of her grandmother's house, where she had first learned to hum.

Iris asked nervously whether it was wrong to breathe through her mouth, since she had read that it was a terrible habit. Dev said that this was a myth: during hard exercise, or when the nose is blocked by a cold, the mouth is a perfectly sensible extra door, though it filters and warms the air a little less. He said that the body knows what it needs, and that many popular rules about the nose are stricter than the evidence.

Dev added a note of caution, because waking up often with a dry mouth can sometimes mean that the nose is blocked, or that someone is snoring or breathing noisily in sleep. It is not something to diagnose from the sofa, he said, and a doctor is the right person to find out why, since many causes are easy to treat. Iris wrote the sentence down in her notebook under the heading when to ask for help.

A week after the first rehearsal, Iris arrived with her notebook full of tally marks, small drawings and scribbled observations about her own breathing. She had noticed that it rose high and fast whenever she hurried or checked the time, and that it settled when she stirred her tea without thinking about anything at all. Dev read her pages with real pleasure and said that she now understood the machine, so it was time to look at how she used it.

Dev asked Iris to close her eyes and point to the place where she felt her breath move when she was worried. Without hesitation she pointed to the very top of her chest, close to her collarbones, and she was surprised at how certain she was. It was the first time she had ever described her own breathing from the inside, and it felt almost like giving directions to a house she had lived in for years.

When we are frightened, the body releases adrenaline and other stress hormones, and breathing speeds up and moves towards the top of the chest, ready for running or fighting. That alarm system is useful when there is a real tiger in the room, Dev said, but it is far less useful when the danger is a long phrase in a song. The body, unfortunately, does not always know the difference between a tiger and a tricky bar of music, and it reacts to both.

Dev taught her a very simple exercise, in which Iris sat upright with one hand resting on her chest and the other on her belly, and simply watched which hand moved more. The upper hand rose and fell busily while the lower one lay almost still, which confirmed what she had suspected, and Dev nodded as if she had passed a small test. There is no shame in it, he said, since it is how most people breathe when they are rushed.

Dev asked her to breathe in slowly through the nose and to let the belly move gently outwards, without pushing it or forcing it. Iris tried so hard at first that her stomach bulged like an overfilled balloon, and Dev burst out laughing and told her that no effort was needed. The belly should simply be allowed to move, he said, as the diaphragm moves down beneath it, like a curtain drifting in a breeze.

Dev was careful to say that in a natural, relaxed breath both the chest and the belly move, and that there is no single correct way to breathe that suits every person. What people call belly breathing is simply a way of letting the diaphragm do its full share of the work, and the research on its benefits, he said, is encouraging but modest. Iris appreciated that he never claimed more than he knew, and she trusted him all the more for it.

That evening, Iris lay on her living-room floor with a light book on her belly and set a timer for five minutes, feeling slightly ridiculous. The book rose and fell like a small boat, and by the third minute she realised that her shoulders, which had been hovering near her ears all day, had slowly dropped to the carpet. She did not feel transformed, but she did feel quieter, and that seemed to be enough for one evening.

On the bus the next morning, Iris noticed with a start that she was holding her stomach in tightly, and that she had probably been doing it for years. Many people clench their middle without thinking, often out of a wish to look slim, and the habit stops the belly from moving and keeps the breath trapped high in the chest. She let her muscles go soft, very slowly, and felt her breath drop at once, as if a door had been unlocked.

At the next rehearsal, Mara raised her baton and Iris, with a little prayer, let a low breath drop into her belly before the first note. It worked for a few glorious bars, her voice rolling out steady and warm, but by the second page her old quick, high breathing had crept back in without asking permission. She was disappointed, but Dev, who was sitting at the back, gave her a thumbs up.

Dev found Iris afterwards and told her not to be discouraged, because a new breathing habit is like a new scale in that it needs repeating over and over before it becomes natural. The old habit would return again and again, he said, since it had been practised for years, and the aim was not to win every time but to notice and come back. She said that this sounded very like what Mara always said about singing in tune, and she felt a little better.

Dev set her the homework for the coming days, which was five quiet minutes of gentle breathing twice a day, lying down or sitting, without forcing anything and stopping if it felt uncomfortable. He added a line he always repeated, that anyone who often feels breathless for no clear reason should see a doctor, because exercises are no substitute for a check-up. Iris copied it into her notebook, drew a small box around it and promised herself that she would never skip that rule.

Dev asked what might happen if a person deliberately slowed the breath, and he explained that researchers have been curious about this for decades. Many of the studies have looked at about six breaths a minute, which is roughly a third of the speed of a typical adult at rest. He cautioned Iris that the studies were mostly small, and that he would report them exactly as they were.

Dev showed her a simple pattern that she could count on her fingers, which was to breathe in through the nose for four counts and out gently for six. Each breath lasted about ten seconds, so the whole thing added up to roughly six breaths in a minute, and for the first few rounds Iris felt as if she were trying to drink from a very thin straw. By the fifth round, however, her body had quietly found the rhythm, and the straw seemed to widen into a comfortable pipe.

Dev asked Iris to rest two fingers on her wrist and feel her pulse while she breathed slowly, and after a minute she gave a small gasp of discovery. Her heartbeat quickened a little on each in-breath and slowed a little on each out-breath, a rhythm that she had never noticed in thirty years of carrying a pulse around. This is perfectly normal, Dev told her, and in healthy people it is a sign of a flexible heart.

A long wandering nerve called the vagus runs from the brain down through the neck to the heart, lungs and gut, and one of its jobs is to slow the heartbeat when it is active. Its signals vary with each breath, which is part of the reason why the pulse rises and falls as we breathe in and out. Dev stressed that scientists understand only part of this story and that it would be wrong to treat the nerve like a switch.

Some researchers suggest that a long out-breath, longer than the in-breath, may nudge the body towards a calmer state, since the slowing of the heart is strongest then. Dev was careful to point out that the evidence for this is modest, and that Iris should treat the idea as a pleasant experiment rather than as a promise. She liked the way he said it, which made her feel she was a scientist in her own small laboratory.

Dev summarised what the research has shown so far, which was that some small studies found slow breathing lowered feelings of stress or blood pressure by modest amounts. Other studies found little change at all, and many were short, used different methods or lasted only a few weeks, so it is hard to draw firm conclusions. He told her that this is how real science usually looks, with patterns that are interesting but not yet settled.

Dev warned Iris that the internet is full of videos promising to hack the vagus nerve, to reset the whole body in a minute or to cure all kinds of troubles with a single breath. These claims almost always go much further than the science can support, he said, and anyone who sounds completely certain about complicated biology deserves a little suspicion. Iris underlined the word modest in her notebook, because it seemed to be Dev's favourite word, and she was starting to see why.

Iris began a little diary in which she drew a face and wrote a line after each session of slow breathing. On some days she felt calm and a little sleepy, on others she felt nothing special, and once she felt faintly annoyed at the whole thing, which Dev said was perfectly normal and rather useful to know. The honest record, he told her, was worth far more than a hopeful one, because only an honest record could show her what truly helped.

At the next rehearsal Mara paused beside Iris and remarked, with a raised eyebrow, that she seemed rather calmer than she had a week before. The long phrase in Snow Light still caught her out, and her breath ran dry a good beat before the end, but this time she laughed instead of freezing, and the laughter itself seemed to loosen her chest. It was a small thing, but Iris noticed it, and she carried the feeling home like a warm coin in her pocket.

Dev summed up the lesson of the week by saying that slow breathing is a gentle tool, that six breaths a minute is not a magic number, and that each person should find the pace which feels comfortable and easy. If it ever feels forced, strained or dizzy, he added, the right move is to stop and breathe normally, because nothing in this book is worth a headache. Iris promised that she would listen to her own body first, and to every video on the internet a long way afterwards.

On a cool afternoon, Iris and Dev sat on a bench in the Park, where the leaves were coming down in slow spirals around them. She told him about a morning on a crowded station platform, years before, when she had felt dizzy and her fingers had started to tingle and she had been convinced that something terrible was happening. Dev listened without interrupting, and then he said that he knew exactly what she meant.

Dev explained that what she described has a name, hyperventilation, which simply means breathing in a way that is faster or deeper than the body needs at that moment. The result is that too much carbon dioxide is blown away, and the chemistry of the blood shifts slightly, even though there is plenty of oxygen. Iris was startled, because she had always imagined that big breaths were good for her.

When carbon dioxide falls too low, some blood vessels in the brain narrow and the chemistry of the blood changes in ways that the nerves notice. The result can be dizziness, tingling in the fingers or around the lips, muscle tightness and a strange, floating sense of unreality, all of which are harmless in themselves but extremely alarming. Dev said that the body is only being clumsily protective, and that the sensations pass once the breathing settles.

One of the cruellest tricks of fast breathing, Dev told her, is that it can leave a person with a desperate feeling of not getting enough air, even though they are taking in plenty. The natural response is to breathe faster still, which makes matters worse, and so a small wobble can grow into a frightening spiral within a minute. Iris nodded slowly, because the description matched her morning on the platform exactly, right down to the tingling.

Fast breathing is also a common part of panic, Dev said, and a panic attack can feel so frightening that people think they are in grave danger, even though the episode itself usually passes within minutes. He made it very clear that he could not diagnose anything on a park bench, and that anyone who has frequent panic attacks, or who is not sure what is happening, should talk to a doctor. Help is available for people who suffer from them, he said, and it works well for many of them.

Iris asked about the old trick of breathing into a paper bag, which she had seen in a dozen films and cartoons. Dev said that doctors no longer recommend it, because it can lower oxygen too far, and because the cause of someone's breathlessness is not always what it seems. It was a good example, he added, of a piece of advice that everyone knew and trusted, and that turned out to be wrong after a closer look.

In the moment, Dev said, it may help to sit down, relax the shoulders and let the breath slow, with a gentle out-breath that is a little longer than the in-breath. He added a firm warning that if the feeling is new, if it is severe, or if there is chest pain, it should never be put down to nerves, and medical help should be sought straight away. Iris copied this down very carefully, because she knew that she would be tempted to skip it when she felt well, and she did not want to.

Before the next rehearsal, Iris stood alone in the wings with her eyes closed and breathed slowly, with a long, soft out-breath that seemed to carry some of her worry away with it. She felt steadier than usual, though she knew perfectly well that she was not cured, and that the tight feeling would probably come back when Mara lifted her baton. She decided that steadier was a perfectly good thing to be, at least for this particular week.

In the corridor, Sam, a friendly tenor with a wicked sense of humour, admitted that almost every singer in the choir felt sick before a concert, and that he himself ate a banana and hummed. Iris was amazed, because she had always believed that she was the only one, and the discovery made her feel strangely lighter. Talking about it, Sam said, was half the cure, and she thought that this might well be true, even if it could not be measured.

As the light faded over the Park, Dev told Iris that she was not repairing a fault, because there was no fault, but building a skill, which is something quite different. The Winter Concert was only four weeks away, he reminded her, and that was enough time to become a little steadier, though not enough to become a different person. Iris laughed and said that she would settle very happily for steadier, and then she thanked him for the bench, the leaves and the patience.

Dev drew a large square on the whiteboard and wrote the number four beside each of its sides, then tapped the first corner with his marker. This, he said, was box breathing, a pattern in which a person breathes in, holds, breathes out and holds again, with the same count for each part. Iris copied the square carefully into her notebook, as though the shape itself might help her, and wrote four small fours beside it.

Iris traced the square in the air with one finger as she counted, in for four, hold for four, out for four and hold for four. The pauses felt strange and slightly tense, as if she were waiting for a lift that did not arrive, so she shortened the count to three and found it much easier. Dev nodded and said that this was exactly the right thing to do, since the count should suit the person.

Some people find the equal counts steadying, Dev explained, partly because counting gives a busy mind a simple, absorbing job to do, and partly because the slow rhythm may help the body settle. He was honest that nobody has shown the box pattern to be better than any other slow pattern, so it should be chosen for comfort and not for any special power. Iris smiled, since she was learning that this kind of honesty was Dev's favourite trick, and that it made his advice easier to trust.

Iris admitted that she did not enjoy the holds, because they reminded her of the sensation she was trying to escape on the platform. Dev said immediately that she could skip them altogether and simply breathe slowly in and slowly out, which is, after all, what most of the studies looked at. There was no rule, he added, that said a breathing exercise must be difficult to be useful.

Dev showed her another pattern, which he called cyclic sighing, and which has a pleasing simplicity to it. A person breathes in through the nose until the lungs are nearly full and takes a second short sip of air on top, and then comes a long, slow breath out through the mouth, like a deep sigh of relief. Iris said that it was the most natural thing she had ever been told to do.

Dev told her about one trial that compared different five-minute daily breathing practices, in which cyclic sighing lifted mood a little more than one of the other methods. He stressed that this was a single study, that the differences were small, and that scientists would need many more trials before anyone could say with confidence what works for whom. It is promising and interesting, he said, but it is not a promise, and Iris should enjoy the sigh without expecting a miracle.

At home that evening, Iris sat on the edge of her bed and tried cyclic sighing for five minutes by the clock, with her phone face down beside her. The long breath out felt like a real sigh of relief, the kind that one gives on taking off a heavy coat, and she ended the practice feeling pleasantly quiet and a little sleepy. She wrote a smiling face in her diary and then, truthfully, a small question mark.

Dev reminded her that no pattern is magic, and that the box, the sigh and the simple slow breath are all different ways of doing one thing, which is helping a person to pay gentle attention to the breath. The best pattern, he said, is the one that a person finds comfortable and is willing to repeat, since a technique that is never used cannot help anyone. Iris thought that this was possibly the most useful sentence she had heard all month.

Dev added a short list of safety rules, the first of which was that anyone who feels dizzy, faint or unwell during an exercise should stop at once and go back to normal breathing. People with heart or lung conditions, and women who are pregnant, should ask a doctor before trying anything stronger than gentle, comfortable breathing, he said, especially long holds or forceful fast breathing. These rules were not meant to frighten her, he said, but to keep her safe and let her enjoy the practice without worry, which mattered much more.

At the end of the lesson, Iris opened her notebook to a fresh page and wrote a short list of the tools she had gathered so far: the low breath, the long out-breath and the double sigh. She read it twice, feeling a quiet pride that had little to do with the concert and a great deal to do with the simple discovery that she was no longer helpless. Dev, who was tidying the whiteboard at the other side of the room, pretended not to notice her smile, though he was clearly pleased.

Before rehearsal, Sam waved his phone at Iris and showed her a video in which a confident man promised that one simple breathing trick would cure stress, transform sleep and add years to her life. Iris was curious and a little tempted, so she took the claim straight to Dev at their next meeting, rather as a child takes a strange insect to a teacher. Dev watched the whole video without once changing his expression, and then he reached calmly for a marker and the whiteboard.

Dev drew a ladder on the whiteboard with three rungs, which he labelled strong evidence, modest evidence and weak evidence, and he explained that every health claim deserves to be placed on one of them. Strong evidence comes from many large, careful studies that agree with each other, while weak evidence comes from stories, guesses or very small experiments. Most breathing claims, he said, sit on the lower two rungs, and a few of the loudest ones sit on the bottom.

Many videos claim that a special style of breathing will detox the entire body, and Dev said that this is where the science stops and the marketing begins. Breathing removes carbon dioxide, which is certainly a waste product, but the liver, kidneys and gut deal with most of the rest, and there is no good evidence that a breathing exercise adds to their work. He suggested that Iris be wary of any claim that uses the word detox without saying exactly what is being removed.

Another popular claim is that breathing more deeply and more often will flood the body with extra oxygen and give a person more energy. Dev explained that in a healthy person at rest the blood is already almost fully loaded with oxygen, so breathing harder cannot add much. It may even upset the balance of carbon dioxide, as Iris had learned on the park bench, because the body is not an empty tank waiting to be filled.

Dev said, with unusual firmness, that no breathing technique has been shown to cure a serious disease, and that videos which suggest otherwise can do real harm. Exercises of this kind may help some people to feel a little calmer or more comfortable as an extra, alongside proper treatment, but nobody should ever stop taking a medicine because of something they saw online. Iris wrote the sentence in her notebook and drew a bold line beneath it.

Dev spoke with particular care about methods that combine a burst of very fast breathing with a long breath-hold, which have become popular online. Some small studies have looked at them with interest, he said, but people have fainted while practising, and some have been badly hurt. They should never be done in water, while driving or anywhere that a fall would matter, and Iris decided that this was one trend she would happily leave to somebody else.

Dev gave Iris four questions to carry about with her whenever she met a claim, and he counted them out on his fingers. Who is saying it, how many people were studied, was the result compared with anything, and who makes money if she believes it? Iris tried them at once on Sam's video and was amused to find that the confident man failed on three of the four.

Dev added that the opposite mistake is just as bad, because modest evidence is not the same as no evidence, and dismissing everything would be as foolish as believing everything. Slow breathing has real, if limited, support from careful studies, and it costs nothing and carries little risk for most healthy people, so it deserves a fair trial. Honesty, he said, has to cut in both directions, or it is not honesty at all.

At the next rehearsal Iris took her low breath, let her shoulders hang and began the long phrase of Snow Light with her eyes on Mara's baton. This time she made it almost to the end, with her breath running out only on the very last word, and when the choir cut off together, Mara looked straight at her and gave a small, delighted nod. Iris felt as if she had climbed a steep hill and found a wide, bright view waiting at the top, and she did not mind the missing last word.

Walking out of the hall into the dark, Dev said that they had reached the halfway point and that it was a good time to take stock. The science of how the lungs and diaphragm work is very solid, he said, while the science of what breathing exercises can do is promising but more modest. The honest message would sit somewhere between those two facts, and there were still three weeks before the concert, and a great deal left to learn.

Mara, who had heard a great deal about Dev from Iris, invited him to the next rehearsal to talk to the whole choir about breathing. Singers need long, controlled out-breaths, she said, so singing is already a kind of breathing workout, and she was curious to hear what a lung specialist made of it. Dev, delighted, arrived early with a folder of drawings and a large bag of paper cups.

Dev told the choir that the voice begins in the larynx, a short tube at the top of the windpipe that holds the vocal folds, two small flaps of tissue that lie on either side. When air from the lungs rushes between them they vibrate hundreds of times a second, and that vibration is the raw sound which the mouth and throat then shape into words and music. Without the breath, he said, a voice has nothing to work with, which is why a singer's first instrument is the lungs.

A long note, Dev explained, depends on letting the breath leave very slowly and evenly, which is a more skilful job than it sounds, since the lungs naturally want to spring back. Voice teachers call this breath support, and many of them tell singers to keep the ribs wide while the air trickles out. Dev admitted that scientists still argue about exactly which muscles do what, and that the images teachers use are often more useful than strictly accurate, so a singer should keep whichever image helps.

Between phrases, singers must breathe in very quickly and silently, with no time to fuss, and Mara said that a good quick breath feels like a small happy surprise. It should drop low into the body, through the mouth and nose together, rather than being snatched up into the shoulders, and Iris realised with a jolt that her old habit was exactly the opposite. The catch breath, as Mara called it, was something that could be learned like any other skill.

Mara led a warm-up that sounded like a roomful of motorboats, in which everybody blew air through relaxed lips to make a bubbling noise called a lip trill. The trick is that the air must be perfectly steady or the lips stop vibrating, so the exercise teaches control without any effort, and Iris, who found it ticklish, collapsed into giggles after four seconds. Dev said that laughing was no bad thing, since a laugh is simply another way of breathing, and a rather good way of loosening the chest.

Mara asked everyone to breathe in and make a long, quiet hissing sound, counting the seconds silently until the air was gone, and the rows of singers hissed like a nest of friendly snakes. Iris managed fourteen seconds, which was neither a triumph nor a disaster, and Dev quietly reminded her that numbers like this are useful only for comparing oneself with oneself, and that nobody should ever push on until they feel dizzy. It is a measure of practice, he said, and not a test, and the numbers will change from one day to the next without any fuss.

Mara told the singers to take out their pencils and mark a small comma in the score wherever they planned to breathe, because a plan is the surest cure for a surprise. In a choir, she explained, nobody is expected to hold a note to the end of a long line, because singers can breathe at slightly different moments so that the music never seems to stop. Iris stared at her score, thinking that this was something she had never been taught.

With a small shock, Iris realised that the long phrase in Snow Light had never been meant to be sung in one breath. She could slip in a quiet, quick breath in the middle, just as the singers beside her did, and she pencilled a comma after the word light. Dev, listening from the back, wrote something short in his own notebook and smiled, as if he had expected it all along.

Dev mentioned that singing in a group is enjoyed by a great many people, and that a number of small studies suggest it may lift well-being. The evidence is modest and hard to separate from the pleasure of meeting friends, he said, and nobody needs a research paper to tell them that a choir is a good thing to belong to. The choir, who had been listening closely and rather enjoying themselves, burst into warm and entirely spontaneous applause.

Dev finished with a few simple reminders for people who use their voices a great deal, which were to drink water, to rest between rehearsals and not to sing through pain. A voice that stays hoarse for several weeks, he added, should always be checked by a doctor, since persistent hoarseness has many possible causes and few of them can be sorted out at home. Mara thanked him warmly, handed him a large cup of tea and promised him a front-row seat at the concert, which he accepted with pleasure.

In the quiet rehearsal room, Dev asked Iris to close her lips, hum a low, steady note and rest her fingertips lightly on the sides of her nose. A ticklish buzz at once ran under her fingers, as if a small bee had settled there, and she broke into a fit of laughter that ruined the note. Dev waited, grinning, and told her to begin again, because the hum was the next piece of the puzzle.

A hum, Dev explained, is really just a long, gentle out-breath with a sound riding on top of it, and the sound itself forces the breath to slow down. There is no need to count seconds or keep track of a pattern, since the breath is already being shaped by the note, which makes humming a pleasant tool for people who dislike counting. Iris admitted that she was one of them, and that this was suspiciously good news.

Dev told her about one small study in which researchers measured the nitric oxide in people's noses and found that humming raised it much more than quiet breathing did. The result was real and interesting, he said, but it came from few people and a short experiment, and nobody can yet say what, if anything, it means for health. He wanted her to enjoy the hum without hanging any big promises on it.

At home that evening, Iris sat in her kitchen and hummed the lullaby that her grandmother used to sing over a steaming teapot, and she was startled by what happened next. Her breath slowed all by itself without any counting, her shoulders softened, and a warm and quiet feeling spread across her chest. It seemed that some of the best breathing lessons had been given to her years ago, long before anyone had thought to call them lessons.

Dev suggested a simple routine that Iris could repeat a few times a day, which was to breathe in gently through the nose for a count of four and then hum out for as long as felt comfortable. For most people that comes to six or eight counts, he said, but the length did not matter, and the hum should never be strained, pushed or squeezed. Iris promised herself that she would stop at the very first hint of discomfort, and that she would never make a competition of it.

Iris tried humming very quietly at a cold bus stop, feeling certain that the whole street would stare at her. A small dog looked up with great interest, and an old man in a flat cap smiled and nodded as if she had passed a test, and she realised that hardly anyone minds a hum. She was struck by how much of her old worry had been about being watched, rather than about her breathing itself.

Mara began the next rehearsal with a humming warm-up, sliding gently up and down the scale with her mouth closed and her hand on her cheekbone. The buzz in the front of the face, she told them, helps singers find an easy, forward sound before they open their mouths. It is also gentler on the voice than diving straight into a loud song, she added, and Iris felt the hum in her cheeks and could not stop smiling.

Dev added a warning, because some websites claim that humming can treat sinus problems or even clear infections, and none of that has been proved. A person with facial pain, a long-lasting blocked nose or a fever should see a doctor rather than hum and hope, he said, since the humming may be pleasant but it is not a medicine. Iris wrote this on the same page as the paper-bag warning and drew a small star.

In the corridor, Iris showed Sam the humming routine, and he, being a tenor with a taste for the dramatic, produced a note so deep that it rattled a window. The singers waiting nearby joined in one by one until the whole corridor was humming, and it dissolved at last into a warm, buzzing laughter that Iris suspected did everyone as much good as the breath itself. Nobody, afterwards, could remember exactly who had begun it, and nobody cared in the least.

Two weeks before the Winter Concert, Iris noticed, while washing a cup, that her stomach was not tied in a knot. She felt less afraid than she had a month earlier, and while she knew the fear had not vanished, she could see that it had grown a little smaller and a good deal quieter. Dev, when she told him, said that this is how practice works, in tiny steps that are easy to miss until one looks back.

In the clinic, Dev noticed that Iris had slid down into her chair with her shoulders rounded and her chin pushed forward, a posture that she clearly assumed at her desk all day. He asked her, kindly, whether she thought the way a person sits could change the way a person breathes, and Iris, who spent hours typing in a small office, suddenly felt rather caught out. She admitted, with a rueful laugh, that she had never thought about it for a single moment in her whole life.

Dev explained that a slumped posture can limit how freely the ribs and the diaphragm are able to move, because the chest is folded and the belly has less room to expand. Some studies have measured small differences in lung function between slumped and upright sitting, and the effect, he said, is real but modest, and not worth losing sleep over. It is a nudge and not a rule, Dev said, and the body is wonderfully adaptable when it is given the chance to move.

Sitting tall gives the chest a little more room to expand, Dev said, but the aim is ease and not stiffness, and no one should sit as if they were a soldier on parade. He suggested imagining a thread attached to the top of her head, lifting gently towards the ceiling while her shoulders remained soft and her jaw relaxed. Iris tried it and was astonished to feel her breath settle lower, almost at once.

At work the next morning, Iris stuck a note on her screen and set a gentle chime on her phone to ring every hour. The slump kept creeping back, naturally, and by lunchtime she was folded like a letter in an envelope. Dev told her that each reminder was a small success, that she should treat herself with the kindness she would offer a friend, and that the habit would arrive slowly.

Dev told her that no single posture is perfect, and that the best posture is always the next one, because moving often matters more than holding any position for hours. People who sit for long periods are advised by many health bodies to stand, stretch and walk now and then, he said, and a short break is good for the back, the mind and the breath alike. Iris pledged, with her notebook open, to leave her desk at least once every hour and to walk to the window.

Dev showed Iris a gentle side stretch that could be done at any desk, in which she raised one arm above her head and leaned slowly to the side. As she breathed in, she felt the ribs on the stretched side widen and open like a fan, a sensation that she had never noticed before, and she was surprised at how much space there was in her own body. He warned her that any stretch should feel comfortable and never painful, and that she should stop at once if it did.

Iris learned to roll her shoulders slowly back and down in a circle, then let them hang loose like coats on a peg, and to let her neck lengthen and her jaw unclench. These small movements ease the tension that crept into her upper body whenever she was nervous, and they make it easier for the lower ribs to do their share of the breathing. She did them three times before a long email, again before lunch, and once more on the bus home, feeling lighter each time.

At rehearsal, Mara told the choir to stand with their feet about hip-width apart and their knees soft, never locked, because standing rigid for a long time can leave a person feeling faint. It is a surprisingly common problem on stage, she said, and every choir has a story about someone who went down quietly in the middle of a quiet song. The sopranos nodded solemnly, with the air of people who had seen it happen more than once and had never forgotten it.

Dev pointed out that looking down at a phone for hours can round the shoulders and bend the neck forward, which leaves the chest a little more cramped. Holding the phone higher, changing position and taking breaks may help, he said, although the research on this is modest and he did not want to turn a normal habit into a terrible sin. Iris glanced guiltily at her own phone, which was lying face up on the desk, and then slid it quietly into her bag.

Dev closed the lesson by saying that posture is a helper and not a cure, and that Iris should not trouble herself about getting it perfect, because a relaxed, moving body matters far more than a statue-like back. She smiled, rolled her shoulders once more and walked out into the cold evening with her chin level and her chest a little more open. Four weeks earlier she would not have noticed any of it, and now she could feel every small change.

On a cold Saturday morning, Dev took Iris to the Park and set off at a brisk pace up the steepest hill, with his scarf flapping behind him. The best way to understand breathing during exercise, he told her over his shoulder, is to feel it with your own lungs, and she was too busy puffing to argue. By the third lamp post, she could hear her own breath rushing like a small wind.

When the leg muscles work hard they burn more fuel, so they use more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide. The brain notices the change through its sensors, and it tells the diaphragm and the other breathing muscles to work faster and harder, which is why the breath grows louder on a hill. Iris realised that she was watching, in real time, the whole story that Dev had drawn on the whiteboard a month before.

During exercise, breathing grows both faster and deeper at the same time, so the amount of air moving in and out each minute rises sharply. In hard exercise it can climb to many times the resting level, Dev said, which is a splendid example of the body matching its supply to its demand without anybody having to decide anything. Iris, panting beside him, remarked that she would have liked to decide to stop for a moment.

Dev taught her a simple method called the talk test, which needs no equipment at all. If she could talk in full sentences but not sing, the effort was moderate, which is right for most people, and if she could only gasp out a few words at a time, then she should slow down and recover. Iris, a singer, found this very funny, and promptly tried to sing a line from Snow Light to check.

On the steepest part of the hill, Iris noticed that she had given up on her nose altogether and was breathing hard through her open mouth. She felt a flash of guilt, remembering the conversation about nasal breathing, but Dev laughed and told her that it was perfectly sensible, since the body needs a wider doorway when the demand for air is high. It would be odd, he added, to insist on a narrow door during a rush.

In the cold air, Iris could see her breath leave her mouth in puffs of white, like the smoke from a tiny, friendly dragon. Dev explained that every out-breath is warm and carries water vapour from the lungs and airways, and that when it meets cold air the vapour condenses into tiny drops of water that we can see. It was a small fact, but she found herself loving how visible her breath had become.

Dev mentioned that cold, dry air can make some people cough or feel tight in the chest, and that a loose scarf over the nose and mouth can warm the air a little and help. If a person regularly wheezes or feels chest tightness during exercise, however, it is something to ask a doctor about and not something to push through, because it can be a sign of a condition that can be treated. Iris, who had never wheezed, nodded and filed the advice away carefully in her mind for any friends who might need it.

Dev smiled and said that here, at last, was a claim near the top of his evidence ladder: regular exercise helps the heart, the lungs and the muscles to work together more efficiently. Over weeks and months, the same effort feels easier and the breath settles sooner afterwards, and this is supported by a great many large and careful studies. He seemed delighted to be able to say that something in the field was truly well established.

At the top, Iris sat on a cold bench and felt her breath gradually slow, her pulse dropping from a gallop to a canter and then to a walk. How quickly the breath and heartbeat settle after effort is one rough sign of a person's fitness, Dev told her, though he would not want her to start timing herself and worrying. She wrapped her hands around a warm cup from his flask and gazed at the grey city below.

On the hilltop, with the city spread out below her like a map, Iris took a low breath and hummed a long note, and she was pleased to find it steadier than anything she could have managed a month earlier. Dev glanced at his calendar and told her that there were only twelve days left until the Winter Concert, and Iris felt a flutter that was not entirely fear. She decided that it was just as likely to be excitement, and that she might as well enjoy it.

In the clinic, Dev took down a framed photograph of a high mountain pass, with tiny figures trudging across a field of snow, and told Iris that he had walked it on holiday years before. He had been fit and well, he said, yet near the top he had felt as breathless as a man twice his age, and he had stopped every few steps to gasp. The photograph, he added, was the reason he had become interested in breathing at all.

Dev explained that the air on a mountain has the same mix of gases as the air by the sea, with about a fifth of it oxygen, and that the difference is in the pressure. Higher up there is less air above to press down, so the air is thinner, and each breath contains fewer oxygen molecules than the same breath would at sea level. It is as if the air had been sold in smaller bottles, he said, though the price stays the same.

On the highest mountains in the world, the air pressure is only about a third of what it is at sea level, so each breath carries only about a third of the oxygen. Climbers at those heights often take bottled oxygen, Dev said, and even the strongest of them move very slowly, as if they were wading through deep water. Iris imagined taking a breath of that air and felt a small shiver run down her back.

When people climb high, the body responds at once, because sensors in the neck and brain detect the thinner air and send urgent signals to the breathing muscles. Breathing becomes faster and deeper, and the heart beats faster to move the oxygen around, which is why even a gentle walk at altitude can feel like running. Dev said that it was a perfect example of the same system working that Iris had been studying, only turned up to a high setting.

Over days and weeks, Dev said, the body adapts to the thin air in a process called acclimatisation, in which breathing patterns settle and the body makes more red blood cells to carry more oxygen. This takes time, which is why hikers and mountaineers are advised to go up slowly and to rest on the way, so that the body has a chance to catch up. Iris thought that this was a good lesson for anyone who was in a hurry, about mountains or anything else.

Dev added a serious warning about altitude sickness, which can cause headaches, nausea, tiredness and poor sleep, and which in a few cases becomes dangerous. If symptoms get worse, the right response is to stop climbing, go down to a lower height and seek medical help, and anyone planning a trip to high places should ask a doctor or a local guide for advice first. He had no wish to turn a pleasant holiday into a story with a sad ending.

In some parts of the world, such as the high plateaus of the Andes, Tibet and Ethiopia, whole communities have lived at great heights for many generations. Scientists have found that their bodies show certain differences that seem to help them cope with thin air, though the details vary from place to place and there is still a great deal to learn. Dev said that this shows how flexible the human body can be over long stretches of time.

Iris asked whether the special training masks and altitude tents that she had seen advertised were worth buying. Dev said that the evidence for them is mixed, that elite athletes sometimes use altitude training for particular reasons, and that for most ordinary people the answer is probably not. A good walk in the Park costs nothing, he said, and is supported by a great deal more research.

Dev mentioned that the air in an aeroplane cabin is also kept at a lower pressure than the air at sea level, so passengers are, in effect, spending a few hours on a modest mountain. Most healthy people never notice it, he said, but people with certain lung or heart conditions should ask their doctor before they fly, since the thinner air can matter for them. Iris, who liked to travel, made a careful note of this in her notebook for the sake of her friends.

That evening, Iris stood at her window with a mug of tea, looking at the faint line of hills in the distance and thinking about what Dev had said. Her breath depended on the air around her and on the place where she lived, and on a whole chain of small, clever processes inside her body, and she realised that she no longer took any of it for granted. It was a quiet kind of wonder, and it suited her very well indeed.

On a hazy morning, Dev met Iris at the clinic window and pointed to the grey smear hanging over the rooftops. All the care in the world about how we breathe, he said, means little if the air itself is full of things that irritate the lungs, and so the quality of the air deserves a lesson of its own. Iris had been so busy looking inwards that she had barely thought about the sky.

Dev explained that very fine particles from traffic, factories, smoke and wood fires are so small that they can travel deep into the lungs, past some of the defences that guard the nose and the upper airways. The mucus, the cilia and the cough catch a great many of them, he said, but nothing in the body is perfect, and a steady supply of dirty air puts those defences under strain. Iris pictured her little brushes working overtime in a smoky room, and she felt quite sorry for them.

Polluted air can irritate the airways and make asthma and some heart conditions worse, Dev said, and large studies have linked long-term exposure to a higher risk of a number of health problems. He was careful to say that these are patterns across large groups of people and not predictions for any one person, and that for most healthy adults an occasional hazy day is not a cause for alarm. The aim is to reduce exposure sensibly, he said, not to live in fear.

Dev reminded her that people spend most of their time indoors, so the air inside a home matters as much as the air outside it. Opening a window now and then, switching on the fan when cooking and treating damp patches can all help, since mould and damp can irritate the airways of some people, particularly those who already have asthma or allergies. Iris looked at the corner of her bathroom ceiling in her mind and made a note to deal with it.

When it is possible, Dev suggested, people should walk or exercise along quieter streets or through parks and away from the busiest roads, where exhaust fumes are thickest. On days when the air is poor, many towns publish air-quality reports that can help people choose when and where to be active, and sensitive people may prefer to take it easy indoors. He admitted cheerfully that none of this was glamorous, but it was sensible and cost almost nothing.

Dev explained that cigarette smoke damages the cilia, slowing their sweeping, and irritates the airways, which then make extra mucus and cough. Over many years it can contribute to serious lung diseases, and Iris at once thought of her uncle Tom, a cheerful man who had smoked for forty years and had always been short of breath on the stairs. She remembered him sitting on the garden bench at family parties, quietly catching his breath.

The encouraging fact, Dev said, is that stopping smoking helps at any age, and that many of the benefits begin sooner than people expect, from better circulation to a gradually quieter cough. Iris told him that Tom had stopped at sixty, after a scare at the bus stop, and that he now claimed that stairs felt easier and that food tasted better than it had for decades. Dev smiled and said that stories like that were the very best argument for trying.

Dev added that no one has to stop smoking alone, because health services offer advice, medicines, support groups and telephone helplines that can double a person's chances of success. Many people need several attempts before they stop for good, he said, and a relapse is part of the process and not a sign of weakness, so nobody should give up trying. He spoke without the slightest hint of a lecture, and Iris liked him all the more for it.

Iris asked about vaping, and Dev replied that it is much newer than smoking, so its long-term effects are still being studied. It is not harmless, he said, and people who do not smoke should not start. A doctor can advise a smoker about whether it might help them to stop, since the picture is complicated and the evidence is still changing, and as always Dev was more comfortable saying what was unknown than pretending to know.

That evening, Iris telephoned her uncle Tom and invited him to the Winter Concert, which was only ten days away. He was delighted, promised to wear his best scarf, and said, with a chuckle that rattled slightly, that he would be the proudest man in the hall. Iris put the phone down feeling warm, and happily aware that a good listener in the second row would make the whole evening easier.

In the corridor before rehearsal, Sam took a small inhaler from his pocket, used it carefully and put it away again as casually as a man checking his watch. He told Iris that he had asthma, that he had had it since childhood and that it had never stopped him from singing, and Iris, who had known him for years, realised that she had never once asked. It struck her how much of other people's breathing we never see, and how much we simply assume.

Dev explained that in asthma the lining of the airways becomes inflamed and swollen, and the small muscles around the tubes can tighten, so the passages narrow and extra mucus may collect. The result is a whistling sound called a wheeze, along with coughing, a feeling of tightness in the chest and sometimes breathlessness, which can come and go from day to day. Asthma is common, he said, and the severity varies enormously from one person to another.

Asthma is managed with a plan drawn up by a doctor or a nurse, Dev said, and it usually includes a reliever inhaler for sudden symptoms and sometimes a daily preventer that calms the inflammation over time. Sam followed his plan faithfully, using his inhaler exactly as he had been taught, and he told Iris that knowing what to do made the condition feel like something he could manage rather than something that managed him. Dev nodded and said that this is precisely how it should work for everyone who has asthma, and that no one should have to guess.

Different things can set off asthma in different people, Dev said, and the usual suspects include colds, pollen, dust mites, cold air, smoke and hard exercise, though everyone has a particular list. Sam knew his triggers very well, and he planned around them with the practical good humour of a man who has done so for years. It made Iris think of the many invisible skills that lie behind an ordinary evening at a choir rehearsal.

Dev said that breathing exercises may help some people with asthma to feel a little better, as an extra alongside their medicines, but he stressed that the evidence is modest and varies from study to study. They are an addition and never a replacement, he said, and nobody should change or stop their medicines because of an exercise or a video without talking to their doctor or nurse first. Sam said, with a grin, that he would keep his inhaler and add a hum.

Dev spoke slowly and very clearly, because this was the most important thing he would say all week. A person who is severely breathless, who cannot speak in full sentences, whose lips look blue or whose reliever inhaler is not helping needs emergency help at once. The right action is to call the emergency services without delay and not to wait and see, and Iris wrote it down in capital letters and added the number that she would need.

Dev mentioned a surprising fact, which was that many people do not use their inhalers quite correctly, so that less of the medicine reaches the airways than it should. It is well worth asking a pharmacist or a nurse to watch and check the technique, he said, since a small adjustment such as using a spacer can make a real difference. Sam, who had been shown properly years ago, said that he would ask for a refresher anyway.

In the middle of a sentence, Iris coughed and apologised, and Dev said at once that there was no need, because a cough is one of the body's most useful defences. It is a sudden burst of air, driven by the muscles of the chest and abdomen, that blows dust, mucus and other irritants out of the airways. A body that could not cough would be in a good deal of trouble, he said, and it is only when a cough lingers that it needs any attention at all.

Most coughs that follow a cold, Dev said, fade within a few weeks, but a cough that lasts about three weeks or longer should always be checked by a doctor. So should one that brings up blood, or that comes with weight loss, fever or breathlessness, he added, because these are signs that deserve a proper examination rather than a guess. Iris, who liked rules that she could remember, wrote three weeks on a card and pinned it to her wall.

As they walked back to the rehearsal, Sam told Iris that he was glad she had not made a fuss about his asthma, since people so often treated it as either nothing or a catastrophe. They shared the banana in the corridor, laughing, and agreed that both of them were rather better at singing than they were at being scared. There was only a week to go until the concert, and neither of them could have said which of them felt more cheerful about it.

With six days to go, Iris lay awake in the small hours, listening to the clock and rehearsing every possible disaster in her head. The next day, tired and rather crumpled, she asked Dev what her breathing did while she was asleep, and whether it might have something to do with the way she felt. He said that it was a very good question, and that the night shift of the lungs deserved its own lesson.

Dev explained that breathing changes through the night, becoming slower and very regular during deep sleep and more variable and uneven during the dreaming phases. The brainstem keeps the whole thing going without any help from the sleeper, he said, although the muscles of the throat relax a little, which is part of the reason why some people snore. Iris found it oddly touching to think of her body quietly keeping watch while she dreamed.

Dev said that slow, quiet breathing in bed may help some people to relax and drift off, and that a few small studies point that way, though the evidence is modest and results vary. It costs nothing and carries little risk for most healthy people, so Iris might as well try it, he said, with the lights low and the phone far away. That night, she did exactly that, and she was asleep before she had finished counting the third long out-breath.

Dev added that he was a lung physiotherapist and not a sleep expert, so Iris should treat his advice as a small piece of a much larger picture. Simple habits such as a regular bedtime and a dark, quiet room help many people, he said, but poor sleep that goes on for weeks is worth discussing with a doctor, who can look for the cause and suggest treatment. It is a common problem, and no one needs to struggle through it alone.

Dev explained that snoring is the sound of the soft tissues at the back of the throat vibrating as air flows through a narrowed space, much like a flag flapping in a wind. The throat muscles relax in sleep, and some people have narrower airways than others, or a blocked nose, or sleep flat on their backs. It is very common and often quite harmless, he said, though it is rarely harmless to the person in the next pillow.

Dev went on to explain that loud snoring with pauses in the breathing may be a sign of a condition called sleep apnoea, in which the airway narrows or closes repeatedly during the night. People with it often feel very tired during the day or wake with headaches, he said, and no one should try to guess, because a doctor can arrange tests and the condition can be treated effectively. Iris wrote down the pattern in her notebook, since she knew that she would be asked about it by half the choir.

Often, Dev said, it is a partner, a friend or a family member who notices the pauses in breathing, because the sleeper is of course asleep and knows nothing about it. Anyone who is told that they stop breathing, snore loudly or gasp in their sleep should take it seriously and see a doctor, since sleep apnoea is common, easy to miss and well worth treating. Sam, who was listening, admitted cheerfully that he snored like a tuba and promised to ask somebody.

Dev mentioned a trend that he had seen online, in which people tape their mouths shut at night in the hope of sleeping better and breathing through the nose. There is little good evidence that it helps, and it could be unsafe, particularly for anyone with a blocked nose or a condition such as sleep apnoea, so he did not recommend it. A person who cannot breathe comfortably through the nose at night needs a doctor, he said, and not a roll of tape.

Dev added that for some people who snore, sleeping on the side instead of the back can reduce the noise, since lying flat lets the tongue and soft tissues fall backwards towards the throat. The effect varies from person to person, he said, and it is no replacement for medical advice if sleep apnoea is suspected, but it is an easy thing to try. Iris, who slept on her back, resolved to roll over that very night and to report back to him the next day.

Iris gave a huge yawn in the middle of a sentence, and Dev, who could not help catching it, laughed and admitted that science has no firm answer to why we yawn. Several ideas have been suggested, such as cooling the brain or changing our level of alertness, and yawning is certainly catching, but none of the explanations has been proved to everyone's satisfaction. He said that he found it comforting that something as ordinary as a yawn could still be a mystery.

In the waiting room, a mother was rocking a newborn baby who had begun to cry, and Dev, stopping beside Iris, pointed out that she was hearing a very ordinary miracle. Before birth the lungs are filled with fluid, and in the first minutes of life the fluid drains or is absorbed while the baby takes its first breaths, and the first cry helps to open the air sacs. Iris looked at the tiny red face and was surprised to feel her eyes sting.

Dev explained that babies and young children breathe much faster than adults, because their lungs are small and their bodies burn a great deal of fuel for their size. As they grow, the rate slowly falls until it reaches the adult range, and Iris realised that the baby's quick, shallow breaths would have been alarming in a grown man but were perfectly right for a newborn. What counts as normal depends greatly on who is breathing, Dev said, and on how old they are.

The lungs grow through childhood and the teenage years and work at their best in early adulthood, usually around the mid-twenties, Dev told her. After that, lung capacity declines slowly with age, in a gentle slope that most people never notice, because the lungs have a great deal of spare capacity built in. Iris, in her thirties, found it reassuring that she had so long still to go along that slope, and said so.

The best-supported advice of all, Dev said, is to stay active throughout life, because regular movement helps the heart, the lungs and the muscles to go on working well. Walking, dancing, swimming, singing and climbing stairs all count, and there is strong evidence for the general benefits of activity, even though it is hard to say precisely how much any one kind of exercise helps the lungs. He added that it is never too late to start, and rarely too early.

Iris watched Edith, the oldest alto in the choir, who was eighty-one and sang the long phrases of Snow Light on a steady breath that Iris could only envy. Dev, standing beside her, said that regular singing and activity are good for people of any age, but that anyone, young or old, who notices new or worsening breathlessness should always see a doctor. Edith winked at them across the hall, apparently aware that she was being discussed.

Dev's final lesson was about habit, and it was a modest one that anybody could manage. A few minutes of slow, gentle breathing a few times a day, he suggested, perhaps on waking, after lunch and before bed, will do more good than an hour of effort once a month. Iris pinned a note to her mirror and promised to be kind to herself on the days when she forgot, and the days that she remembered would then count for more.

Dev and Iris sat down and wrote a simple plan for the day of the concert on the back of a card. It included a gentle walk in the morning, a hum in the wings, a low breath before the first note and a quiet, quick breath exactly where Mara had marked it in the score. Dev insisted that it be short and kind, because a plan that was too complicated would only become another thing to worry about.

Before the dress rehearsal, Mara surprised Iris by asking her to lead the warm-up, and Iris, her cheeks pink, stood at the front of the choir and led the lip trills and the humming. The whole choir followed her, bubbling and buzzing, with Sam's bass note rolling underneath it all. Halfway through she realised that she was the one teaching, which would have seemed quite impossible six weeks earlier, and Dev, at the back, looked very pleased.

At the dress rehearsal, with the lamps on and the hall almost empty, Iris took her low breath and sang the long phrase of Snow Light, slipping in her quiet breath exactly where she had pencilled it. The line flowed out smooth and unbroken, and Mara, who had been watching from the front, beamed and gave a small, private nod of approval, which Iris had waited all her singing life to receive. Nobody else even noticed the breath, which was the whole point of taking it at the right place.

On the night before the concert, Dev walked Iris to the bus stop and told her that she had not been fixed, because there was never anything wrong with her in the first place. She had learned a skill, he said, and some fear before a performance is normal and even helpful, since it sharpens the senses and brings the body to life. Iris laughed and said that she would keep a little of it, as long as it stayed in the second row.

On the morning of the Winter Concert, Iris woke early, read her card and followed her plan, beginning with a gentle walk through the frosty Park. She hummed as she went, watching her breath float away in white clouds, and she felt nervous but not frightened, which she thought was a distinction worth remembering. A message from Dev appeared on her phone, which said only, breathe low and enjoy it.

By evening the town hall had begun to fill with people in heavy coats, stamping the cold from their boots and chatting in warm, rising waves. Iris peeked through the curtain and saw her uncle Tom waving his best scarf in the fourth row and Dev settling into the front seat that Mara had promised him. It was a strange comfort to know exactly where her two supporters were sitting.

Backstage, with ten minutes to go, Iris felt the familiar signs begin, her heart quickening and her breath turning quick and high, as if somebody had pressed a button. She noticed them, and instead of fighting them, she recognised them for what they were: the old alarm, ringing a little loudly, and nothing worse. She almost smiled at it, the way one might greet an old friend who always arrives early.

Iris used her tools one after another, starting with the low breath, then a slow count of four in and six out, then a soft hum that she hardly needed to count at all. Sam, beside her, rolled his eyes comically and breathed with her, and old Edith reached over and squeezed her hand with a dry, warm grip. By the end of the second minute the hammering had faded to a gentle knock.

The choir filed onto the stage beneath the warm lamps, and the murmuring audience gradually fell silent, until the hall seemed to be holding its own breath. Iris took her place in the second row with her knees soft, her shoulders low and her feet planted firmly, exactly as Mara had taught them in the weeks before. Mara raised her hands, and in the half-second before the first note, Iris let a slow, low breath fall into her belly.

The first songs went well, and Iris, listening to her own voice as it blended into the choir, noticed that her breath was rising and falling in an easy rhythm without any effort at all. The music seemed to carry her along like a gentle current, and between songs she let the out-breath settle slowly, almost forgetting that she had ever been afraid. Somewhere in the fourth row, she knew, a man in a long scarf was beaming.

Then came Snow Light, the last song of the programme, and with it the long phrase that had caused her so much trouble. Iris took her low breath, sang the first half with a steady, open tone, slipped in her quiet breath exactly where she had marked it, and sang on, and the line flowed out as smooth as a ribbon of silk. When the phrase ended she still had a little air left over, which astonished her.

The final chord drifted up into the rafters and faded, and for a long moment nobody in the hall moved or breathed. Then the audience rose and the applause broke over the stage like a wave, rolling on and on, and Iris saw her uncle Tom on his feet, clapping with both hands above his head and his scarf waving. She was smiling so widely that she felt her breath catch, and for once she did not mind.

Over tea in the empty hall after the concert, Dev told Iris that breathing is a useful tool and not a cure for everything, and that the greatest thing she had gained was the habit of noticing it. Her breath was always with her, he said, and she could return to it in a crowded train, before an interview or in the quiet of her bed. Nothing in the last six weeks had required a gadget, a subscription or a secret, only a little attention.

Iris and Dev sat together in the quiet hall as the lights were lowered one by one, and for a minute neither of them said anything at all, only breathed. This book has offered only general information, and the science of breathing is still growing, so it is not medical advice and cannot take the place of a doctor who knows you. If you are worried about your breathing, your lungs or your health, please speak to a medical professional, and then take one more slow, easy breath.
